cards.note: *And being but one, she can do all things: and remaining in herself, she makes all things new: and in all ages entering into holy souls, she makes them friends of Yahuah (God), and prophets.* Wisdom 7:27 names the Spirit's anointing-of-prophets pattern — *she makes them friends of Yahuah, and prophets.* The dove-descent at Matt 3:16 is the same Spirit's anointing of the Servant-Prophet-King the Father will name at v.17.
cards.s_text: And Yahusha (Jesus), when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of Elohim (God) descending like a dove, and lighting upon him:
cards.t_text: And being but one, she can do all things: and remaining in herself, she makes all things new: and in all ages entering into holy souls, she makes them friends of Yahuah (God), and prophets.

cards.note: *He professeth to have the knowledge of Yahuah (God): and he calls himself the child of Yahuah (God).* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:13). *And when the tempter came to him, he said, If thou be the Son of Elohim (God), command that these stones be made bread.* (Matthew 4:3). The ungodly in Wisdom of Solomon fasten on one claim, that the righteous man calls himself the child of Yahuah (God), and they set out to test it: *if the just man be the son of Yahuah (God), he will help him* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:18). The tempter in the wilderness uses the same handle, if you are the Son of Elohim (God), prove it, command the stones. The test comes back at the cross in the same words, *If thou be the Son of Elohim (God), come down from the cross* (Matthew 27:40). The claim of sonship is what the ungodly cannot leave alone, and the devil was the first to pick it up.
cards.s_text: And when the tempter came to him, he said, If you be the Son of Elohim (God), command that these stones be made bread.
cards.t_text: He professeth to have the knowledge of Yahuah (God): and he calls himself the child of Yahuah (God).

cards.note: *We are esteemed of him as counterfeits: he abstaineth from our ways as from filthiness: he pronounceth the end of the just to be blessed, and makes his boast that Yahuah (God) is his father.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:16). *And saith unto him, If thou be the Son of Elohim (God), cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning thee: and in their hands they shall bear thee up, lest at any time thou dash thy foot against a stone.* (Matthew 4:6). The ungodly resent one thing above the rest: the righteous man makes his boast that Yahuah (God) is his father. In the wilderness the tempter picks up the same grievance and turns it into a dare — if you are the Son of Elohim (God), prove it, throw yourself down and let the angels catch you. The claim of sonship is treated as something to be tested by a display of rescue. Yahusha (Jesus) did not take the dare, because sonship is shown by doing the Father's will, not by forcing the Father's hand.
cards.s_text: And says unto him, If you be the Son of Elohim (God), cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning you: and in their hands they shall bear you up, lest at any time you dash your foot against a stone.
cards.t_text: We are esteemed of him as counterfeits: he abstaineth from our ways as from filthiness: he pronounceth the end of the just to be blessed, and makes his boast that Yahuah (God) is his father.

cards.note: *For if the just man be the son of Yahuah (God), he will help him, and deliver him from the hand of his enemies.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:18). *And saith unto him, If thou be the Son of Elohim (God), cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning thee: and in their hands they shall bear thee up, lest at any time thou dash thy foot against a stone.* (Matthew 4:6). Wisdom puts the test in the mouths of the ungodly: if he really is the son of Yahuah (God), then his Father will have to rescue him. The devil carries the same test into the wilderness almost word for word — if thou be the Son of Elohim (God), cast thyself down, and let the angels bear thee up. He even cuts a line out of Psalm 91 to make the dare sound like scripture. The writer of Wisdom had heard this voice centuries before; the gospel shows whose voice it is.
cards.s_text: And says unto him, If you be the Son of Elohim (God), cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning you: and in their hands they shall bear you up, lest at any time you dash your foot against a stone.
cards.t_text: For if the just man be the son of Yahuah (God), he will help him, and deliver him from the hand of his enemies.

cards.note: *Let us condemn him with a shameful death: for by his own saying he shall be respected.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:20). *Then the devil leaveth him, and, behold, angels came and ministered unto him.* (Matthew 4:11). The plot against the righteous man in Wisdom ends in a death sentence; the plot against Yahusha (Jesus) in the wilderness ends with the devil leaving and angels ministering to him. The two are not in conflict. The wilderness was the opening move, not the last one — the enemy withdrew to come back through other hands. Wisdom names the whole arc from reproof to shameful death; Matthew 4 is where that arc begins in the gospel, and it does not end until the cross.
cards.s_text: Then the devil leaveth him, and, behold, angels came and ministered unto him.
cards.t_text: Let us condemn him with a shameful death: for by his own saying he shall be respected.

cards.note: *But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of Yahuah (God), and there shall no torment touch them.* (Wisdom of Solomon 3:1). *Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness’ sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.* (Matthew 5:10). Wisdom's third chapter answers its second. The ungodly tortured and condemned the righteous, and here is where the righteous ended up: in the hand of Yahuah (God), where no torment can reach them. Yahusha (Jesus) says the same to those persecuted for righteousness' sake — the kingdom is theirs. The persecution lands on the body and goes no further. What Wisdom promised the just man, the King promised everyone who would be hated for walking as he walked.
cards.s_text: Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness’ sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
cards.t_text: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of Yahuah (God), and there shall no torment touch them.

cards.note: *They that put their trust in him shall understand the truth: and such as be faithful in love shall abide with him: for grace and mercy is to his saints, and he has care for his elect.* (Wisdom of Solomon 3:9). *Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you.* (Matthew 5:12). Wisdom closes its word to the persecuted righteous with what they have coming: understanding of the truth, abiding with him, grace and mercy to his saints, and his care over his elect. Yahusha (Jesus) says the same to his disciples — rejoice, for great is your reward in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets before you. The disciples are being added to the line of the prophets who were hated for speaking the Father's word, and the care and reward Wisdom promised the elect is laid up for them in the same place.
cards.s_text: Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you.
cards.t_text: They that put their trust in him shall understand the truth: and such as be faithful in love shall abide with him: for grace and mercy is to his saints, and he has care for his elect.

cards.note: *Accustom not your mouth to swearing; neither use thyself to the naming of the Holy One.* (Ecclesiasticus 23:9). *Again, ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto Yahuah (Lord) thine oaths:* (Matthew 5:33). Sirach tells his son not to let his mouth grow used to swearing, nor to make a habit of naming the Holy One. Yahusha (Jesus) begins from what they had heard said of old — do not forswear yourself, perform your oaths to Yahuah (Lord) — and goes on to say swear not at all, let your yes be yes and your no be no. He is not loosening the Torah on oaths; he is cutting away the habit Sirach warned of, the casual oath that made the name common and the word cheap. Speech that is true needs no oath to prop it up.
cards.s_text: Again, you have heard that it has been said by them of old time, You shall not forswear thyself, but shall perform unto Yahuah (Lord) your oaths:
cards.t_text: Accustom not your mouth to swearing; neither use thyself to the naming of the Holy One.

cards.note: *For as a servant that is continually beaten shall not be without a blue mark: so he that sweareth and nameth Yahuah (God) continually shall not be faultless.* (Ecclesiasticus 23:10). *But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is Elohim's (God’s) throne:* (Matthew 5:34). Sirach says a servant who is beaten every day is never without a bruise, and a man who swears and names Yahuah (God) continually is never clean of fault — the habit leaves its mark. Yahusha (Jesus) says swear not at all, not even by heaven, because heaven is the throne of Elohim (God). To swear by heaven lightly is to drag the throne into common talk. The mark Sirach describes is what casual swearing does to a man, and the command in Matthew is how it stops.
cards.s_text: But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is Elohim's (God’s) throne:
cards.t_text: For as a servant that is continually beaten shall not be without a blue mark: so he that sweareth and nameth Yahuah (God) continually shall not be faultless.

cards.note: *A man that useth much swearing shall be filled with iniquity, and the plague shall never depart from his house: if he shall offend, his sin shall be upon him: and if he acknowledge not his sin, he makes a double offence: and if he swear in vain, he shall not be innocent, but his house shall be full of calamities.* (Ecclesiasticus 23:11). *But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.* (Matthew 5:37). Sirach traces what much swearing does to a man: he is filled with iniquity, the plague does not leave his house, and every oath sworn in vain adds to the account. Yahusha (Jesus) names the root in one line — whatever is more than yes and no comes of evil. The iniquity Sirach saw filling the swearer's house and the evil Yahusha (Jesus) names at the source are the same thing seen from two ends. Plain speech, yes and no, is the way out of both.
cards.s_text: But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these comes of evil.
cards.t_text: A man that useth much swearing shall be filled with iniquity, and the plague shall never depart from his house: if he shall offend, his sin shall be upon him: and if he acknowledge not his sin, he makes a double offence: and if he swear in vain, he shall not be innocent, but his house shall be full of calamities.

cards.note: *But by such works have you taught your people that the just man should be merciful, and have made your children to be of a good hope that you give repentance for sins.* (Wisdom of Solomon 12:19). *But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;* (Matthew 5:44). Solomon says the Father's dealings with Yashar'el's (Israel's) enemies were themselves the lesson: by such works he taught his people that the just man should be merciful, and gave his children good hope that he gives repentance for sins. The King teaches the same lesson from the same source. Love your enemies, bless those who curse you, pray for those who persecute you, and the reason follows in the next verse: so that you may be children of your Father, who does exactly that. The mercy the children show is learned from watching the Father show it.
cards.s_text: But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;
cards.t_text: But by such works have you taught your people that the just man should be merciful, and have made your children to be of a good hope that you give repentance for sins.

cards.note: *For if you did punish the enemies of your children, and the condemned to death, with such deliberation, giving them time and place, by which they might be delivered from their malice:* (Wisdom of Solomon 12:20). *That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.* (Matthew 5:45). Even the enemies of his children, even those already condemned to death, he punished with deliberation, giving them time and place to be delivered from their malice. The King points at the sky for the same pattern: the Father makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. The wicked are still being given daylight and harvest, which is time and place to turn. Children who love their enemies in this age are copying a Father who has been doing it since before the land was given.
cards.s_text: That you may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he makes his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust.
cards.t_text: For if you did punish the enemies of your children, and the condemned to death, with such deliberation, giving them time and place, by which they might be delivered from their malice:

cards.note: *Prayer is good with fasting and alms and righteousness. A little with righteousness is better than much with unrighteousness. It is better to give alms than to lay up gold.* Tobit 12:8 names the prayer-fasting-alms triad explicitly in the Hebrew library — the same three Tanakh-substantial practices Matt 6:1-18 walks the display-vs-secret diagnostic across. The architecture of the triad is not a New Testament innovation; the angel Raphael names it as a single righteous-life register at the close of Tobit's narrative, and the Sermon walks the same three at the motive-level.
cards.s_text: Take heed that you do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise you have no reward of your Father which is in heaven.
cards.t_text: Prayer is good with fasting and alms and righteousness. A little with righteousness is better than much with unrighteousness. It is better to give alms than to lay up gold:

cards.note: *The offering of the righteous makes the altar fat, and the sweet savour thereof is before the Most High.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:6). *That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly.* (Matthew 6:4). Sirach says the offering of the righteous makes the altar fat and its sweet savour rises before the Most High. Yahusha (Jesus) says alms given in secret are seen by the Father who sees in secret, and he rewards them openly. The altar is the same in both: it is the Most High who receives, and he receives what is righteous, not what is displayed. An offering made for men to see never reaches that altar; the one made where only he looks is the sweet savour.
cards.s_text: That your alms may be in secret: and your Father which sees in secret himself shall reward you openly.
cards.t_text: The offering of the righteous makes the altar fat, and the sweet savour thereof is before the Most High.

cards.note: *The sacrifice of a just man is acceptable. and the memorial thereof shall never be forgotten.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:7). *That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly.* (Matthew 6:4). Sirach says the sacrifice of a just man is accepted and its memorial is never forgotten. Yahusha (Jesus) says alms given in secret are seen by the Father, who repays openly. The reward of being seen by men is spent the moment it is received; the memorial Sirach speaks of is kept by the Most High, who does not forget. The just man's offering goes into a record that outlasts him.
cards.s_text: That your alms may be in secret: and your Father which sees in secret himself shall reward you openly.
cards.t_text: The sacrifice of a just man is acceptable. and the memorial thereof shall never be forgotten.

cards.note: *Forgive your neighbour the hurt that he has done to you, so shall your sins also be forgiven when you prayest.* (Ecclesiasticus 28:2). *And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.* (Matthew 6:12). Sirach says forgive your neighbour the hurt he did you, and then your own sins will be forgiven when you pray. That is the petition Yahusha (Jesus) taught his disciples to pray, forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors, and the condition is the same in both. Pardon received and pardon extended are named in one breath, in the same act of prayer. The disciples' prayer was not a new idea in Yashar'el (Israel); the wise had been teaching sons to pray this way for generations.
cards.s_text: And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
cards.t_text: Forgive your neighbour the hurt that he has done to you, so shall your sins also be forgiven when you prayest.

cards.note: *One man bears hatred against another, and does he seek pardon from Yahuah (God)?* Sirach 28:3 names the diagnostic in question-form — the hatred-bearer cannot rightly seek the Father's pardon. Matt 6:14's *if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you* walks the same architecture in proposition-form: the receiving of forgiveness from the Father presupposes the extending of forgiveness to the brother. The Hebrew library carries the diagnostic; the gospel binds it as kingdom-citizens grammar.
cards.s_text: For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you:
cards.t_text: One man bears hatred against another, and does he seek pardon from Yahuah (God)?

cards.note: *He sheweth no mercy to a man, which is like himself: and does he ask forgiveness of his own sins?* (Ecclesiasticus 28:4). *But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.* (Matthew 6:15). Sirach presses the question down to the heart: a man shows no mercy to another man, one made like himself, and then asks forgiveness for his own sins? Yahusha (Jesus) answers it in the Sermon: if you forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive yours. The brother who is like you is the test. The heart that withholds mercy from him has no standing to ask it from the Father, and the wise in Yashar'el (Israel) had been saying so long before the disciples' prayer was taught.
cards.s_text: But if you forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.
cards.t_text: He sheweth no mercy to a man, which is like himself: and does he ask forgiveness of his own sins?

cards.note: *For you layest up a good treasure for thyself against the day of necessity.* Tobit 4:9 names the architecture Matt 6:20 walks directly: *but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven.* The Hebrew library's phrasing is the precise gospel-architecture in the gospel's own grammar — *lay up treasure against the day.* Tobias gives alms now; the treasure laid up is what stands when the day of necessity comes. The gospel walks the same architecture at the kingdom-citizens level.
cards.s_text: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust does corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
cards.t_text: For you layest up a good treasure for thyself against the day of necessity.

cards.note: *Because that alms do deliver from death, and suffers not to come into darkness.* (Tobit 4:10). *But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:* (Matthew 6:20). Tobit tells his son that alms deliver from death and keep a man out of the darkness; the open hand protects the giver in the day of necessity. Yahusha (Jesus) says to lay up treasure in heaven, where moth and rust do not corrupt and thieves do not break through. Both are talking about what cannot be lost. Tobit names the deliverance the open hand brings; the gospel names the storehouse the open hand fills, and nothing gets in to spoil it.
cards.s_text: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust does corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
cards.t_text: Because that alms do deliver from death, and suffers not to come into darkness.

cards.note: *Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High, and it shall bring you more profit than gold.* (Ecclesiasticus 29:11). *But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:* (Matthew 6:20). Sirach says lay up your treasure the way the commandments of the Most High direct, and it will profit you more than gold. Yahusha (Jesus) says lay up for yourselves treasure in heaven, where moth and rust and thieves cannot reach. The two are the same counsel: the hand that opens to the brother and the poor because the commandment says so is laying up the treasure the King means. The treasure in heaven is kept by keeping the commandments on earth.
cards.s_text: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust does corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
cards.t_text: Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High, and it shall bring you more profit than gold.

cards.note: *Shut up alms in your storehouses: and it shall deliver you from all affliction.* Sirach 29:12 names the storehouse-of-alms architecture — the treasure laid up against affliction. The Hebrew library uses the same *storehouse* image the gospel uses at *treasures in heaven.* Matt 6:20 walks the same Hebrew library architecture: the kingdom-citizen who lays up alms in the heavenly storehouse is delivered from the loss the earthly storehouse cannot protect against.
cards.s_text: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust does corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
cards.t_text: Shut up alms in your storehouses: and it shall deliver you from all affliction.

cards.note: *Give Yahuah (God) his honour with a good eye, and diminish not the firstfruits of yours hands.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:8). *The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.* (Matthew 6:22). Sirach tells the worshipper to give Yahuah (God) his honour with a good eye and not to cut short the firstfruits of his hands. The good eye is an old Hebrew way of speaking of generosity, the eye that is not grudging and does not measure what it gives. Yahusha (Jesus) speaks of the single eye that fills the whole body with light, and the verses around it are about treasure and about mammon. A good eye in giving and a single eye in the body are the same eye; it looks at Yahuah (God) and his honour, and the hand follows where it looks.
cards.s_text: The light of the body is the eye: if therefore your eye be single, your whole body shall be full of light.
cards.t_text: Give Yahuah (God) his honour with a good eye, and diminish not the firstfruits of yours hands.

cards.note: *The envious man has a wicked eye; he turns away his face, and despiseth men.* (Ecclesiasticus 14:8). *But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!* (Matthew 6:23). Sirach calls envy a wicked eye and says the man who has it turns away his face and despises men. Yahusha (Jesus) says the evil eye fills the whole body with darkness. In the Hebrew idiom the evil eye is not a vague picture of bad vision; it is the stingy, envious heart that closes its hand and looks away. The King is speaking the idiom Sirach spoke, and the darkness he names is the darkness of the closed hand.
cards.s_text: But if your eye be evil, your whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you be darkness, how great is that darkness!
cards.t_text: The envious man has a wicked eye; he turns away his face, and despiseth men.

cards.note: *A covetous man’s eye is not satisfied with his portion; and the iniquity of the wicked drieth up his soul.* (Ecclesiasticus 14:9). *But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!* (Matthew 6:23). Sirach says the covetous eye is never satisfied with its portion, and that the iniquity dries the soul up. Yahusha (Jesus) says the evil eye leaves the whole body full of darkness. A dried-up soul and a darkened body are two ways of describing one man — the grasping one who never has enough and cannot see by his own light.
cards.s_text: But if your eye be evil, your whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you be darkness, how great is that darkness!
cards.t_text: A covetous man’s eye is not satisfied with his portion; and the iniquity of the wicked drieth up his soul.

cards.note: *A wicked eye envies his bread, and he is a niggard at his table.* (Ecclesiasticus 14:10). *But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!* (Matthew 6:23). Sirach brings the wicked eye to the table: the host who begrudges his own bread even as he serves it. Yahusha (Jesus) asks how great the darkness is when the light itself has gone dark. Bread can cross a table with no blessing in it. The niggard's whole hospitality is darkness, however much he puts out, because the eye behind it is closed.
cards.s_text: But if your eye be evil, your whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you be darkness, how great is that darkness!
cards.t_text: A wicked eye envies his bread, and he is a niggard at his table.

cards.note: *He that loves gold shall not be justified, and he that followeth corruption shall have enough thereof.* (Ecclesiasticus 31:5). *No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon.* (Matthew 6:24). Sirach says the man who loves gold will not be justified. Yahusha (Jesus) says why: no man can serve two masters, and you cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon. The man whose heart holds to gold has already given his service to another master, and he cannot stand justified before a Father whose service is the whole heart. The gold-lover and the mammon-server are the same man seen from two sides.
cards.s_text: No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. You cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon.
cards.t_text: He that loves gold shall not be justified, and he that followeth corruption shall have enough thereof.

cards.note: *Gold has been the ruin of many, and their destruction was present.* (Ecclesiasticus 31:6). *No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon.* (Matthew 6:24). Sirach says gold has ruined many, and their destruction was right there with it. Yahusha (Jesus) sets the choice before his disciples: Elohim (God) or mammon, one master or the other, never both. The disciple who chooses mammon is walking toward the ruin Sirach had already watched overtake many. The wise saw where gold leads; the King made the fork in the road plain.
cards.s_text: No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. You cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon.
cards.t_text: Gold has been the ruin of many, and their destruction was present.

cards.note: *It is a stumblingblock to them that sacrifice to it, and every fool shall be taken with it.* (Ecclesiasticus 31:7). *No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon.* (Matthew 6:24). Sirach speaks of men who sacrifice to gold. He names it as a thing worshipped, an altar men bring offerings to, and he says it trips every fool who goes near it. That is why Yahusha (Jesus) can set mammon across from Elohim (God) as a rival master: mammon in that sentence is not a neutral tool but a master that takes those who serve it, the very stumblingblock Sirach saw men sacrificing to. You cannot keep an altar to both.
cards.s_text: No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. You cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon.
cards.t_text: It is a stumblingblock to them that sacrifice to it, and every fool shall be taken with it.

cards.note: *But the righteous live for evermore; their reward also is with Yahuah (God), and the care of them is with the Most High.* (Wisdom of Solomon 5:15). *Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they?* (Matthew 6:26). The care of the righteous is with the Most High. That is the ground the King stands on when he tells his disciples to look at the birds: they neither sow nor reap nor fill barns, and the heavenly Father feeds them, and you are worth more than they. Taking no anxious thought is not a technique; it is what follows when you know whose care you are already in. Solomon named the care, and the King named the birds so his hearers could see it with their eyes.
cards.s_text: Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are you not much better than they?
cards.t_text: But the righteous live for evermore; their reward also is with Yahuah (God), and the care of them is with the Most High.

cards.note: *Therefore shall they receive a glorious kingdom, and a beautiful crown from the hand of Yahuah (God): for with his right hand shall he cover them, and with his arm shall he protect them.* (Wisdom of Solomon 5:16). *But seek ye first the kingdom of Elohim (God), and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.* (Matthew 6:33). The kingdom and the crown come from the hand of Yahuah (God), and his right hand covers those who receive them. The King tells his disciples to seek that kingdom first and let the rest be added. Food and clothing are the small things the covering hand already holds for the one who is reaching for the kingdom itself; the same arm that protects the righteous in Wisdom is the one the King promises will add all these things.
cards.s_text: But seek you first the kingdom of Elohim (God), and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.
cards.t_text: Therefore shall they receive a glorious kingdom, and a beautiful crown from the hand of Yahuah (God): for with his right hand shall he cover them, and with his arm shall he protect them.

cards.note: *Prosperity and adversity, life and death, poverty and riches, come of Yahuah (God).* (Ecclesiasticus 11:14). *But seek ye first the kingdom of Elohim (God), and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.* (Matthew 6:33). Sirach says both halves come from Yahuah (God) — prosperity and adversity, life and death, poverty and riches. That is the ground under Yahusha's (Jesus's) seek first: if the Father administers both, the citizen does not have to administer either, and can turn toward the kingdom and his righteousness with both hands. The adding comes from the same hand the adversity does.
cards.s_text: But seek you first the kingdom of Elohim (God), and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.
cards.t_text: Prosperity and adversity, life and death, poverty and riches, come of Yahuah (God).

cards.note: *Do that to no man which you hatest: drink not wine to make you drunken: neither let drunkenness go with you in your journey.* (Tobit 4:15). *Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.* (Matthew 7:12). Here is the golden rule in the Hebrew library, in its negative form, from a father to his son generations before the Sermon on the Mount. Yahusha (Jesus) states it positively and then says what it is: *this is the law and the prophets.* He was not bringing a kinder ethic to replace a Torah too hard to keep; he was naming the heart of the Torah that Tobit had already handed to his son. The teaching that the King invented a new religion in place of the law collapses against this one verse in Tobit.
cards.s_text: Therefore all things whatsoever you would that men should do to you, do you even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.
cards.t_text: Do that to no man which you hatest: drink not wine to make you drunken: neither let drunkenness go with you in your journey.

cards.note: *Malice and wrath, even these are abominations; and the sinful man shall have them both.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:30). *Judge not, that ye be not judged.* (Matthew 7:1). Sirach calls malice and wrath abominations and says the sinful man carries both. Yahusha (Jesus) says judge not, that you be not judged, and the next verse tells why: the measure you use is the measure that comes back on you. A man carrying malice cannot judge his brother rightly, because the malice is in the judgment, and the judgment rebounds. Sirach names the heart condition that has to be cleared before any brother can be weighed.
cards.s_text: Judge not, that you be not judged.
cards.t_text: Malice and wrath, even these are abominations; and the sinful man shall have them both.

cards.note: *He that revengeth shall find vengeance from Yahuah (God), and he will surely keep his sins in remembrance.* (Ecclesiasticus 28:1). *For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.* (Matthew 7:2). Sirach says the man who takes revenge will get vengeance from Yahuah (God), and his own sins will be kept in remembrance. Yahusha (Jesus) says it as a rule of measure: with what judgment you judge, you will be judged, and with what measure you mete it will be measured back. The standard a man uses on his brother is the standard the Father uses on him. Sirach had it in the Hebrew library long before the Sermon on the Mount: the revenger writes his own sentence.
cards.s_text: For with what judgment you judge, you shall be judged: and with what measure you mete, it shall be measured to you again.
cards.t_text: He that revengeth shall find vengeance from Yahuah (God), and he will surely keep his sins in remembrance.

cards.note: *If he that is but flesh nourish hatred, who will intreat for pardon of his sins?* (Ecclesiasticus 28:5). *Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother’s eye.* (Matthew 7:5). Sirach asks who will plead for the pardon of a man who is only flesh and yet nurses hatred. Yahusha (Jesus) tells the man with the beam in his own eye to get it out first, and then he will see clearly to help his brother with the mote. The two belong together: the one nursing hatred cannot ask the Father's pardon for himself, and so he cannot rightly help a brother with his fault either. The beam comes out first, and the hatred is the beam.
cards.s_text: You hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of your own eye; and then shall you see clearly to cast out the mote out of your brother’s eye.
cards.t_text: If he that is but flesh nourish hatred, who will intreat for pardon of his sins?

cards.note: *Whoso teaches a fool is as one that glueth a potsherd together, and as he that waketh one from a sound sleep.* (Ecclesiasticus 22:7). *Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.* (Matthew 7:6). Sirach says teaching a fool is like gluing a broken pot back together, or waking a man out of a dead sleep — the effort does not hold. Yahusha (Jesus) says it as a command: do not give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine, because they will trample them and turn and rend you. Both know that some hearers cannot receive, and that the holy thing is wasted and the teacher is harmed when it is pressed on them. The proclamation goes out broadly, but the pursuit ends where the rejection lands.
cards.s_text: Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast you your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.
cards.t_text: Whoso teaches a fool is as one that glueth a potsherd together, and as he that waketh one from a sound sleep.

cards.note: *He that telleth a tale to a fool speaks to one in a slumber: when he has told his tale, he will say, What is the matter?* (Ecclesiasticus 22:8). *Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.* (Matthew 7:6). Sirach says telling a tale to a fool is talking to a man asleep — when you have finished he asks what you were saying. Yahusha (Jesus) sharpens that into a command about the holy things: do not cast pearls before swine, who will trample them and turn on you. The wisdom book had been teaching discernment of the hearer for centuries; the gospel makes it a rule for the citizens of the kingdom. We speak the truth wherever the Father sends us, and when it is refused we shake the dust off and go on.
cards.s_text: Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast you your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.
cards.t_text: He that telleth a tale to a fool speaks to one in a slumber: when he has told his tale, he will say, What is the matter?

cards.note: *Wisdom is glorious, and never fadeth away: yes, she is easily seen of them that love her, and found of such as seek her.* (Wisdom of Solomon 6:12). *Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you:* (Matthew 7:7). Wisdom is found of such as seek her. The King's three verbs, ask, seek, knock, carry the same promise: it will be given, you will find, it will be opened. Solomon adds that she is easily seen of them that love her, which means the seeking is not a long climb but a turning toward what is already in view. The Father gives the good gift to those who ask, and Luke names the gift as the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit) (Luke 11:13), which is the spirit of wisdom Solomon himself prayed for.
cards.s_text: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you:
cards.t_text: Wisdom is glorious, and never fadeth away: yes, she is easily seen of them that love her, and found of such as seek her.

cards.note: *She preventeth them that desire her, in making herself first known to them.* (Wisdom of Solomon 6:13). *Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you:* (Matthew 7:7). Preventeth in the old sense means goes before. Wisdom does not wait to be caught; she goes out ahead of those who desire her and makes herself known first. That is what the King's ask, seek, knock rests on: the disciple is not climbing up to a Father who has to be found, he is knocking on a door the Father is already standing behind. The asking is answered, the seeking finds, the knocking opens, because the one being sought came out to meet the seeker before the seeker set out.
cards.s_text: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you:
cards.t_text: She preventeth them that desire her, in making herself first known to them.

cards.note: *For she goes about seeking such as are worthy of her, sheweth herself favourably to them in the ways, and meeteth them in every thought.* Wisdom 6:16 names wisdom's active pursuit of the seeker — she goes about seeking them, shews herself favourably, meets them in every thought. Matt 7:8's *for every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth* walks the same architecture: the seeking is reciprocated by the Father's standing pursuit of the citizen.
cards.s_text: For every one that asks receives; and he that seeks finds; and to him that knocks it shall be opened.
cards.t_text: For she goes about seeking such as are worthy of her, sheweth herself favourably to them in the ways, and meeteth them in every thought.

cards.note: *The fruit declareth if the tree have been dressed; so is the utterance of a conceit in the heart of man.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:6). *Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?* (Matthew 7:16). Sirach says the fruit tells you whether the tree was dressed, and a man's speech tells you what is in his heart. Yahusha (Jesus) gives the same test for recognizing false prophets: you will know them by their fruits, because thorns do not yield grapes. The test was not new when he gave it; the wise in Yashar'el (Israel) had been teaching it for generations. What the gospel does is hand it to every disciple as the way to know a teacher, so that no one has to be fooled by the costume if he will look at the fruit.
cards.s_text: You shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?
cards.t_text: The fruit declareth if the tree have been dressed; so is the utterance of a conceit in the heart of man.

cards.note: *Praise no man before you hear him speak; for this is the trial of men.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:7). *Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.* (Matthew 7:20). Sirach says do not praise a man until you have heard him speak, because that is where men are tried. Yahusha (Jesus) closes his warning about false prophets the same way: by their fruits you shall know them. A prophet's teaching is his fruit, and a teaching that voids the commandments of Yahuah (God) names the wolf no matter what signs he carries, because Deuteronomy 13 had already said the sign does not excuse the leading away. Hear him speak first; then you know what he is.
cards.s_text: Wherefore by their fruits you shall know them.
cards.t_text: Praise no man before you hear him speak; for this is the trial of men.

cards.note: *As timber girt and bound together in a building cannot be loosed with shaking: so the heart that is stablished by advised counsel shall fear at no time.* (Ecclesiasticus 22:16). *Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:* (Matthew 7:24). Sirach says a heart established by sound counsel is like timber girded and bound into a building — shake it and it does not come loose, so it fears nothing. Yahusha (Jesus) says the wise man is the one who hears his sayings and does them, and he likens him to a house built on a rock. The counsel that establishes the heart is the King's sayings, and the doing of them is what binds the timber. Hearing alone leaves the building loose.
cards.s_text: Therefore whosoever hears these sayings of mine, and does them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:
cards.t_text: As timber girt and bound together in a building cannot be loosed with shaking: so the heart that is stablished by advised counsel shall fear at no time.

cards.note: *A heart settled upon a thought of understanding is as a fair plaistering on the wall of a gallery.* (Ecclesiasticus 22:17). *Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:* (Matthew 7:24). Sirach says a heart settled on a thought of understanding is like fine plaster on the wall of a gallery — finished, smooth, holding. Yahusha (Jesus) says the wise man is the one who hears his sayings and does them, and likens him to a house built on rock. The settled heart and the house on rock are the same man: his heart has come to rest on the King's words, and the building he is stands.
cards.s_text: Therefore whosoever hears these sayings of mine, and does them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:
cards.t_text: A heart settled upon a thought of understanding is as a fair plaistering on the wall of a gallery.

cards.note: *Pales set on an high place will never stand against the wind: so a fearful heart in the imagination of a fool cannot stand against any fear.* (Ecclesiasticus 22:18). *And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.* (Matthew 7:25). Sirach gives the opposite picture: pales set on a height will never stand against the wind, and the fearful heart of a fool cannot stand against any fear. Matthew says the rain came down, the floods came, the winds blew and beat on the house, and it did not fall because it stood on rock. The same wind that cannot move the house on the rock blows the pales flat. The difference is not the wind but the foundation, and the foundation is hearing and doing.
cards.s_text: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.
cards.t_text: Pales set on an high place will never stand against the wind: so a fearful heart in the imagination of a fool cannot stand against any fear.

cards.note: *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning.* (Ecclesiasticus 36:11). *And I say unto you, That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven.* (Matthew 8:11). Sirach prays for all the tribes of Jacob to be gathered and given back their inheritance as from the beginning, twelve tribes and not two. Yahusha (Jesus) says many will come from east and west and sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom. The many from east and west are the children of those three fathers coming home from where they were scattered, which is exactly what Sirach asked for. They are not a new people put in the seat of Yashar'el (Israel); they are the tribes of Jacob taking their own seats at their fathers' table.
cards.s_text: And I say unto you, That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven.
cards.t_text: Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning.

cards.note: *O Yahuah (God), have mercy upon the people that is called by your name, and upon Yashar'el (Israel), whom you have named your firstborn.* (Ecclesiasticus 36:12). *And I say unto you, That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven.* (Matthew 8:11). Sirach prays for mercy on the people called by the name of Yahuah (God), on Yashar'el (Israel) whom he named his firstborn. Yahusha (Jesus) says many will come from east and west and sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom. The firstborn is one people, named from the beginning, and the many from east and west are that firstborn's scattered children coming to their fathers' table. The mercy Sirach asks for the firstborn is the seat Yahusha (Jesus) says they will take.
cards.s_text: And I say unto you, That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven.
cards.t_text: O Yahuah (God), have mercy upon the people that is called by your name, and upon Yashar'el (Israel), whom you have named your firstborn.

cards.note: *Therefore let us lie in wait for the righteous; because he is not for our turn, and he is clean contrary to our doings: he upbraideth us with our offending the law, and objecteth to our infamy the transgressings of our education.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:12). *That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying, Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses.* (Matthew 8:17). Wisdom of Solomon 2 is a long portrait of the righteous one hunted by the ungodly, from the lying in wait here to the shameful death they plan for him in verse 20. Isaiah painted the same man: despised, a man of sorrows, bearing our griefs and carrying our sorrows (Isaiah 53:3–4). Matthew says the healings fulfil that line; the one carrying away the sicknesses of Capernaum is the servant Isaiah saw. He is also the righteous one of Wisdom 2, and the reason the ungodly hate him is given here: his life reproves their breaking of the law. The one who bore our sicknesses was, at the same time, being watched by men who wanted him dead for being righteous.
cards.s_text: That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying, Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses.
cards.t_text: Therefore let us lie in wait for the righteous; because he is not for our turn, and he is clean contrary to our doings: he upbraideth us with our offending the law, and objecteth to our infamy the transgressings of our education.

cards.note: *For if the just man be the son of Yahuah (God), he will help him, and deliver him from the hand of his enemies.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:18). *That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying, Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses.* (Matthew 8:17). The ungodly think the Father's help for his son would look like rescue from the hand of his enemies. Matthew shows what the help actually looked like: the son himself took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses, as Isaiah said he would. The just man who is the son of Yahuah (God) was not spared the suffering; he carried it, and carried it all through his ministry, not only on the last day. Deliverance came, but it came through the bearing and not around it.
cards.s_text: That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying, Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses.
cards.t_text: For if the just man be the son of Yahuah (God), he will help him, and deliver him from the hand of his enemies.

cards.note: *Let us condemn him with a shameful death: for by his own saying he shall be respected.* Wisdom 2:20 names the lawless plotting the shameful death of the just-man — the Hebrew library's explicit precursor to the Isaiah 53 Suffering-Servant's bearing of the despite of the lawless. The healing ministry at Matt 8:16-17 walks the same architecture in its early register: the Servant who will bear the shameful death is currently bearing the infirmities of the people in the towns of Galilee. The Hebrew library's righteous-sufferer architecture is operative across the whole Messianic mission, not collapsed into a single moment.
cards.s_text: That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying, Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses.
cards.t_text: Let us condemn him with a shameful death: for by his own saying he shall be respected.

cards.note: *But your providence, O Father, governeth it: for you have made a way in the sea, and a safe path in the waves;* (Wisdom of Solomon 14:3). *And he saith unto them, Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith? Then he arose, and rebuked the winds and the sea; and there was a great calm.* (Matthew 8:26). The Father's providence governs the sea; he has made a way in it and a safe path in the waves. The Father governs the sea through his Word, the one who made the way in it, and on the lake of Galilee that one was asleep in the stern of a fishing boat while the disciples thought they were dying. He woke, rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. The voice Solomon credits with governing the waters was in the boat in flesh, and the rebuke that calmed the water was the same governance Wisdom had named, exercised from a wet deck by the one who had made the way in the sea in the first place.
cards.s_text: And he says unto them, Why are you fearful, O you of little faith? Then he arose, and rebuked the winds and the sea; and there was a great calm.
cards.t_text: But your providence, O Father, governeth it: for you have made a way in the sea, and a safe path in the waves;

cards.note: *Shewing that you can save from all danger: yes, though a man went to sea without art.* (Wisdom of Solomon 14:4). *And he saith unto them, Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith? Then he arose, and rebuked the winds and the sea; and there was a great calm.* (Matthew 8:26). Solomon says the Father can save from all danger at sea, even a man who went out without the skill to be there. The disciples were fishermen, and the storm outdid their skill anyway; their cry was Lord, save us, we perish (Matthew 8:25). He answered by asking why they were fearful and then rebuking the wind and the water into a great calm. The saving Solomon prayed about was done in front of them, by the one in the boat, and the rebuke of their little faith is that they had the governor of the sea aboard and thought they were on their own.
cards.s_text: And he says unto them, Why are you fearful, O you of little faith? Then he arose, and rebuked the winds and the sea; and there was a great calm.
cards.t_text: Shewing that you can save from all danger: yes, though a man went to sea without art.

cards.note: *He that keepeth the law brings offerings enough: he that takes heed to the commandment offers a peace offering.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:1). *But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* (Matthew 9:13). Sirach says the man who keeps the law has already brought offerings enough, and the one who takes heed to the commandment has offered a peace offering. That is the key to what Yahusha (Jesus) meant by I will have mercy, and not sacrifice, which he took from Hosea. He was not setting mercy against the Torah; mercy is the Torah kept, and the Pharisees who kept the altar while despising the publicans and sinners at his table had kept the smaller part and dropped the greater. The commandment kept is the offering Yahuah (God) wanted all along.
cards.s_text: But go you and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.
cards.t_text: He that keepeth the law brings offerings enough: he that takes heed to the commandment offers a peace offering.

cards.note: *He that requiteth a goodturn offers fine flour; and he that gives alms sacrificeth praise.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:2). *But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* (Matthew 9:13). Sirach says that to repay a good turn is to offer fine flour and to give alms is to sacrifice praise. These are the altar's own words, fine flour and the sacrifice of praise, set on ordinary acts of kindness. When Yahusha (Jesus) told the Pharisees to go and learn what I will have mercy, and not sacrifice means, Sirach had already written out the lesson. Mercy shown is sacrifice offered, and the man who gives alms has stood at the altar whether he knows it or not.
cards.s_text: But go you and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.
cards.t_text: He that requiteth a goodturn offers fine flour; and he that gives alms sacrificeth praise.

cards.note: *To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to Yahuah (God); and to forsake unrighteousness is a propitiation.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:3). *But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* (Matthew 9:13). Sirach says departing from wickedness pleases Yahuah (God) and forsaking unrighteousness is a propitiation; the turning itself is the atonement. Yahusha (Jesus) says he came to call sinners to repentance, not the righteous, in the same breath as I will have mercy, and not sacrifice. The publicans at his table who turned had made the offering Sirach describes; the men standing outside objecting to the company had brought their sacrifices and left the turning undone.
cards.s_text: But go you and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.
cards.t_text: To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to Yahuah (God); and to forsake unrighteousness is a propitiation.

cards.note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). *But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* (Matthew 9:13). Give to the poor and turn your face from none, and the face of Yahuah (God) will not turn from you. That is the mercy Hosea asked for in place of sacrifice, the word Yahusha (Jesus) sends the Pharisees to go and learn. They were offended that he sat at table with sinners (9:11); Tobit had told his son not to turn his face from any poor man. Mercy toward the one in need is the heart of the Torah, and a system that keeps its credentials clean while turning its face away has lost the thing the commandment was for.
cards.s_text: But go you and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.
cards.t_text: Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.

cards.note: *For you layest up a good treasure for thyself against the day of necessity.* (Tobit 4:9). *But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* (Matthew 9:13). Alms laid up are a treasure against the day of need; Tobit sees the open hand as storing something before Yahuah (God). Yahusha (Jesus) tells the Pharisees to go learn Hosea's word, mercy and not sacrifice. They had stored up sacrifices and credentials; the heart of the Torah was the mercy Tobit's son was told to lay up. The treasure that counts in the day of necessity is the mercy that was done, and the King is calling a religious system back to it.
cards.s_text: But go you and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.
cards.t_text: For you layest up a good treasure for thyself against the day of necessity.

cards.note: *Because that alms do deliver from death, and suffers not to come into darkness.* (Tobit 4:10). *But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* (Matthew 9:13). Tobit says alms deliver from death, and he says it in the voice of a father who has lived it. The Pharisees at Matthew's table had their sacrifices in order and their mercy withheld, and the King sent them to Hosea: mercy, and not sacrifice. Tobit had already named mercy as the thing that delivers. A religion that keeps its offerings and loses its mercy has kept the shell and lost the life.
cards.s_text: But go you and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.
cards.t_text: Because that alms do deliver from death, and suffers not to come into darkness.

cards.note: *For alms does deliver from death, and shall purge away all sin. Those that exercise alms and righteousness shall be filled with life:* (Tobit 12:9). *But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* (Matthew 9:13). Raphael's last word to Tobit and Tobias is that alms deliver from death and purge away all sin, and that those who do alms and righteousness are filled with life. This is mercy given the weight of life and death. In Matthew 9 the King forgives a paralytic (9:2) and sits at table with sinners, and when the Pharisees object he sends them to Hosea: mercy, and not sacrifice. Mercy is what the Torah asked for, mercy is what delivers, and the King and the angel are saying one thing.
cards.s_text: But go you and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.
cards.t_text: For alms does deliver from death, and shall purge away all sin. Those that exercise alms and righteousness shall be filled with life:

cards.note: *Give to the godly man, and help not a sinner.* (Ecclesiasticus 12:4). *And it came to pass, as Yahusha (Jesus) sat at meat in the house, behold, many publicans and sinners came and sat down with him and his disciples.* (Matthew 9:10). Sirach says to give to the godly man and not to help a sinner, and the next verse shows what he means — bread given to the ungodly becomes strength he uses against you. Yahusha (Jesus) sat at meat with publicans and sinners. These are not two stances at war. The sinners at that table had come to him, and he was calling them to repentance, not feeding them in their sin. Sirach guards the hand; the King opens the door; and the Pharisee who turned the one into a wall against persons had misread it and could not see the other.
cards.s_text: And it came to pass, as Yahusha (Jesus) sat at meat in the house, behold, many publicans and sinners came and sat down with him and his disciples.
cards.t_text: Give to the godly man, and help not a sinner.

cards.note: *Do well to him that is lowly, but give not to the ungodly: hold back your bread, and give it not to him, lest he overmaster you thereby: for else you shall receive twice as much evil for all the good you shall have done to him.* (Ecclesiasticus 12:5). *And when the Pharisees saw it, they said unto his disciples, Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners?* (Matthew 9:11). Sirach says to do well to the lowly but to hold back your bread from the ungodly, because what you give him he will turn into power over you. The Pharisees asked why the Master ate with publicans and sinners, as if this verse had been broken. It had not. Sirach is warning against strengthening a man in his wickedness; Yahusha (Jesus) was eating with men who had come to hear him and were being called out of theirs. The ungodly in Sirach is the man who stays ungodly with your bread in his hand; the sinner at the King's table is the one who heard and sat down.
cards.s_text: And when the Pharisees saw it, they said unto his disciples, Why eats your Master with publicans and sinners?
cards.t_text: Do well to him that is lowly, but give not to the ungodly: hold back your bread, and give it not to him, lest he overmaster you thereby: for else you shall receive twice as much evil for all the good you shall have done to him.

cards.note: *Give to the good, and help not the sinner.* (Ecclesiasticus 12:7). *But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* (Matthew 9:13). Sirach says it again: give to the good, help not the sinner. Yahusha (Jesus) says he came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance, and he sends the Pharisees to learn what mercy and not sacrifice means. The two verses meet at the word repentance. Sirach withholds help from the sinner who stays a sinner; the King calls the sinner to stop being one, and the mercy he names is the call itself. Neither verse feeds a man in his wickedness, and neither shuts the door on the man who turns.
cards.s_text: But go you and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.
cards.t_text: Give to the good, and help not the sinner.

cards.note: *Prayer is good with fasting and alms and righteousness. A little with righteousness is better than much with unrighteousness. It is better to give alms than to lay up gold:* (Tobit 12:8). *Then came to him the disciples of John, saying, Why do we and the Pharisees fast oft, but thy disciples fast not?* (Matthew 9:14). The angel Raphael tells Tobit and his son that prayer is good with fasting and alms and righteousness, all together, and that a little with righteousness outweighs much without it. John's disciples asked Yahusha (Jesus) why his disciples did not fast as they and the Pharisees did. He does not throw fasting out — he says the days will come when they will fast (9:15) — but he sets it where the angel set it, as one part of a life of mercy and righteousness, not a credential by itself. Fasting alone was never the discipline; fasting with prayer, alms, and righteousness is what the angel taught Tobit and what the King restores.
cards.s_text: Then came to him the disciples of John, saying, Why do we and the Pharisees fast oft, but your disciples fast not?
cards.t_text: Prayer is good with fasting and alms and righteousness. A little with righteousness is better than much with unrighteousness. It is better to give alms than to lay up gold:

cards.note: *So is it with a man that fasteth for his sins, and goes again, and doeth the same: who will hear his prayer? or what does his humbling profit him?* (Ecclesiasticus 34:26). *And Yahusha (Jesus) said unto them, Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? but the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then shall they fast.* (Matthew 9:15). Sirach asks what a man's fast profits him when he fasts for his sins and then goes back and does the same; who will hear his prayer? When John's disciples asked why his disciples did not fast, Yahusha (Jesus) did not do away with fasting; he said the days would come when they would fast. But he placed it after the bridegroom is taken, in the grief of a people who have truly lost something, not as a routine kept while nothing changes. Sirach had already named the difference: a fast that turns from the sin is heard, and a fast that returns to it is noise.
cards.s_text: And Yahusha (Jesus) said unto them, Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? but the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then shall they fast.
cards.t_text: So is it with a man that fasteth for his sins, and goes again, and doeth the same: who will hear his prayer? or what does his humbling profit him?

cards.note: *Forsake not an old friend; for the new is not comparable to him: a new friend is as new wine; when it is old, you shall drink it with pleasure.* (Ecclesiasticus 9:10). *Neither do men put new wine into old bottles: else the bottles break, and the wine runneth out, and the bottles perish: but they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved.* (Matthew 9:17). Sirach honors the old friend and the old wine; the new has to age before it is worth drinking. Yahusha (Jesus) is not quarreling with that. The question put to him in Matthew 9 was about fasting, and his answer is about the vessel: new wine poured into a brittle old skin bursts it and both are lost. The Torah is neither the wine nor the skin; it is the vineyard the wine comes from. The skin that cannot stretch is the body of added tradition, and the wine the King pours will itself grow old and be drunk with pleasure, exactly as Sirach says new wine does.
cards.s_text: Neither do men put new wine into old bottles: else the bottles break, and the wine runs out, and the bottles perish: but they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved.
cards.t_text: Forsake not an old friend; for the new is not comparable to him: a new friend is as new wine; when it is old, you shall drink it with pleasure.

cards.note: *My son, in your sickness be not negligent: but pray to Yahuah (God), and he will make you whole.* (Ecclesiasticus 38:9). *And, behold, a woman, which was diseased with an issue of blood twelve years, came behind him, and touched the hem of his garment:* (Matthew 9:20). Sirach tells the sick man not to be negligent but to pray to Yahuah (God), who will make him whole. The woman with the issue of blood had been sick twelve years, and she came behind Yahusha (Jesus) and touched the hem of his garment, and he turned and told her that her faith had made her whole. She was not going around Sirach's counsel; she was doing it. The one who spoke and walked with the fathers was standing in the crowd in flesh, and reaching for his garment was her prayer to Yahuah (God).
cards.s_text: And, behold, a woman, which was diseased with an issue of blood twelve years, came behind him, and touched the hem of his garment:
cards.t_text: My son, in your sickness be not negligent: but pray to Yahuah (God), and he will make you whole.

cards.note: *Then give place to the physician, for Yahuah (God) has created him: let him not go from you, for you have need of him.* (Ecclesiasticus 38:12). *But Yahusha (Jesus) turned him about, and when he saw her, he said, Daughter, be of good comfort; thy faith hath made thee whole. And the woman was made whole from that hour.* (Matthew 9:22). Sirach does not slight the physician; he says Yahuah (God) created him and tells the sick man to keep him close. The woman with the issue of blood did exactly that for twelve years, and Mark 5:26 adds that she spent all she had on physicians and only grew worse. When she reached for the hem of his garment she was reaching past the physician to the one who made the physician, and Yahusha (Jesus) does not rebuke the years she spent under their care; he names her faith as what made her whole. The physician is a gift from his hand, and the healing was always his.
cards.s_text: But Yahusha (Jesus) turned him about, and when he saw her, he said, Daughter, be of good comfort; your faith has made you whole. And the woman was made whole from that hour.
cards.t_text: Then give place to the physician, for Yahuah (God) has created him: let him not go from you, for you have need of him.

cards.note: *For they shall also pray to Yahuah (God), that he would prosper that, which they give for ease and remedy to prolong life.* (Ecclesiasticus 38:14). *But when the people were put forth, he went in, and took her by the hand, and the maid arose.* (Matthew 9:25). Sirach says the physician himself prays to Yahuah (God) that the remedy in his hand would prosper, because the healing never belonged to the remedy. In the ruler's house the remedies have run out; the girl is dead, and no physician prays over a corpse. Yahusha (Jesus) walks in and takes her by the hand, and the one the physician prays to is the one standing in the room. The physician asks for the prospering; here the giver of it does the work with his own hand.
cards.s_text: But when the people were put forth, he went in, and took her by the hand, and the maid arose.
cards.t_text: For they shall also pray to Yahuah (God), that he would prosper that, which they give for ease and remedy to prolong life.

cards.note: *For you have power of life and death: you leadest to the gates of hell, and bringest up again.* (Wisdom of Solomon 16:13). *He said unto them, Give place: for the maid is not dead, but sleepeth. And they laughed him to scorn.* (Matthew 9:24). Power of life and death belongs to Yahuah (God): he leads to the gates of hell, the grave, and brings up again. In the ruler's house the King looked at a dead girl and said she was not dead but sleeping, and the mourners laughed at him. Then he took her by the hand and she arose. The one who brings up again from the gates of the grave was standing in the room in flesh, and death in his presence is sleep because he is the one who wakes it. The righteous dead are asleep the same way, and the hand that took the girl's hand is the one that will bring them up.
cards.s_text: He said unto them, Give place: for the maid is not dead, but sleeps. And they laughed him to scorn.
cards.t_text: For you have power of life and death: you leadest to the gates of hell, and bringest up again.

cards.note: *A man indeed killeth through his malice: and the spirit, when it is gone forth, returns not; neither the soul received up comes again.* (Wisdom of Solomon 16:14). *But when the people were put forth, he went in, and took her by the hand, and the maid arose.* (Matthew 9:25). The verse draws the line a man cannot cross: he can kill, but once the spirit has gone forth he cannot call it back. Then Yahusha (Jesus) takes a dead girl by the hand and she arises. What Wisdom of Solomon had just said belongs to Yahuah (God) alone — the power of life and death, leading down and bringing up again (16:13) — is done in a house in Capernaum by a man with his hand on a child. That is who he is: not the formless Father, but the one through whom the Father's power has always acted, now standing in flesh.
cards.s_text: But when the people were put forth, he went in, and took her by the hand, and the maid arose.
cards.t_text: A man indeed killeth through his malice: and the spirit, when it is gone forth, returns not; neither the soul received up comes again.

cards.note: *And the lion, whom you sawest rising up out of the wood, and roaring, and speaking to the eagle, and rebuking her for her unrighteousness with all the words which you have heard; This is the anointed, which the Highest has kept for them and for their wickedness to the end: he shall reprove them, and shall upbraid them with their cruelty.* (2 Esdras 12:31–32). *And when Yahusha (Jesus) departed thence, two blind men followed him, crying, and saying, Thou Son of David, have mercy on us.* (Matthew 9:27). Ezra's lion comes up roaring out of the wood and rebukes the eagle, which he had been told is the fourth kingdom Daniel saw (2 Esdras 12:11), and the angel then names the lion: the anointed, kept by the Highest to the end. Two blind men on the road name the same figure by his line, Son of David. The anointed one Ezra saw as a lion, the blind men perceived with no eyes, and they cried out to him as present. The Messiah (Christ) kept for the end was walking past them.
cards.s_text: And when Yahusha (Jesus) departed thence, two blind men followed him, crying, and saying, You Son of David, have mercy on us.
cards.t_text: And the lion, whom you sawest rising up out of the wood, and roaring, and speaking to the eagle, and rebuking her for her unrighteousness with all the words which you have heard;

cards.note: *This is the anointed, which the Highest has kept for them and for their wickedness to the end: he shall reprove them, and shall upbraid them with their cruelty.* (2 Esdras 12:32). *And when Yahusha (Jesus) departed thence, two blind men followed him, crying, and saying, Thou Son of David, have mercy on us.* (Matthew 9:27). The angel tells Ezra what the lion is: the anointed, kept by the Highest to the end, who will reprove the wicked for their cruelty. Two blind men cry to Yahusha (Jesus) as Son of David, the line the anointed king comes from. The one kept to the end to reprove the proud is the one who stops in the road for the blind who ask for mercy. The same anointed, seen by Ezra in a vision and met on a road.
cards.s_text: And when Yahusha (Jesus) departed thence, two blind men followed him, crying, and saying, You Son of David, have mercy on us.
cards.t_text: This is the anointed, which the Highest has kept for them and for their wickedness to the end: he shall reprove them, and shall upbraid them with their cruelty.

cards.note: *For the rest of my people shall he deliver with mercy, those that have been pressed upon my borders, and he shall make them joyful until the coming of the day of judgment, of which I have spoken to you from the beginning.* (2 Esdras 12:34). *And when Yahusha (Jesus) departed thence, two blind men followed him, crying, and saying, Thou Son of David, have mercy on us.* (Matthew 9:27). The anointed does two things in Ezra's vision: he reproves the eagle, and he delivers the rest of the people with mercy, those pressed upon the borders, and makes them joyful until the day of judgment. The blind men ask the Son of David for exactly that, mercy. The remnant pressed at the borders are the scattered of Yashar'el (Israel), and the first work of the Messiah (Christ) toward them is mercy, as it was for the two who cried out. He saw the multitudes as sheep having no shepherd and was moved for them (Matthew 9:36).
cards.s_text: And when Yahusha (Jesus) departed thence, two blind men followed him, crying, and saying, You Son of David, have mercy on us.
cards.t_text: For the rest of my people shall he deliver with mercy, those that have been pressed upon my borders, and he shall make them joyful until the coming of the day of judgment, of which I have spoken to you from the beginning.

cards.note: *For my son the Messiah shall be revealed with those that be with him, and they that remain shall rejoice within four hundred years.* (2 Esdras 7:28). *And when Yahusha (Jesus) departed thence, two blind men followed him, crying, and saying, Thou Son of David, have mercy on us.* (Matthew 9:27). Ezra is told that the Most High's own son, the Messiah, will be revealed, with those that are with him. Two blind men who cannot see him cry out to him on the road as the Son of David and ask for mercy. What was spoken to Ezra as something still coming, they confess as someone present. The one the Most High calls my son and the one the blind men call Son of David are the same man standing in the road.
cards.s_text: And when Yahusha (Jesus) departed thence, two blind men followed him, crying, and saying, You Son of David, have mercy on us.
cards.t_text: For my son the Messiah shall be revealed with those that be with him, and they that remain shall rejoice within four hundred years.

cards.note: *Behold! the days come, and it shall be when the time of the age has ripened, And the harvest of its evil and good seeds has come, That the Mighty One will bring upon them...* 2 Baruch 35:1 names the wisdom-stream's apocalyptic-harvest architecture explicitly — the harvest comes when the time of the age has ripened; the harvest is of evil-and-good-seeds together. Matt 9:37's *the harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few* walks the same architecture at the King's arrival: the harvest the apocalyptic-stream had named as eschatologically-future is now plenteous and present at the King's seeing of the multitudes.
cards.s_text: Then says he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;
cards.t_text: Behold! the days come, and it shall be when the time of the age has ripened, And the harvest of its evil and good seeds has come, That the Mighty One will bring upon the earth and its inhabitants and upon its rulers Perturbation of spirit and stupor of heart.
