Solomon promises to tell what wisdom is and how she came up, to hide no mysteries, to trace her from the beginning of her nativity and bring the knowledge of her into light. The King opens his mouth in parables to utter things kept secret from the foundation of the world. Both are teachers who refuse to pass over the truth; both are bringing into the light what had been hidden, and the parables, which the crowd heard as stories, were that light being given to the disciples who asked what they meant.
cards.s_text: That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying, I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things which have been kept secret from the foundation of the world.
cards.t_text: As for wisdom, what she is, and how she came up, I will tell you, and will not hide mysteries from you: but will seek her out from the beginning of her nativity, and bring the knowledge of her into light, and will not pass over the truth.

cards.note: *And the men that are received shall see it, who have not tasted death from their birth: and the heart of the inhabitants shall be changed, and turned into another meaning.* (2 Esdras 6:26). *That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying, I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things which have been kept secret from the foundation of the world.* (Matthew 13:35). Among the tokens of the end Ezra is told that the heart of the inhabitants will be changed and turned into another meaning, and that men who have not tasted death will see it. When Yahusha (Jesus) teaches in parables he is uttering what had been kept secret from the foundation of the world, and a parable only opens to a heart that has been turned toward its meaning; to everyone else it stays a story about seed and soil. Ezra goes on to hear that the truth so long without fruit shall be declared (2 Esdras 6:28). The parables are that declaring begun, and the changed heart is the one that hears them.
cards.s_text: That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying, I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things which have been kept secret from the foundation of the world.
cards.t_text: And the men that are received shall see it, who have not tasted death from their birth: and the heart of the inhabitants shall be changed, and turned into another meaning.

cards.note: *Wisdom that is hid, and treasure that is hoarded up, what profit is in them both?* (Ecclesiasticus 20:30). *Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.* (Matthew 13:44). Sirach asks what good hidden wisdom or hoarded treasure does anyone — none, until it is found and brought out. Yahusha (Jesus) tells of treasure hidden in a field, and of the man who finds it and sells everything he has to buy the field, because treasure found is worth all of it. The man who buys the field is the one who paid the whole price: the Father, through the Son, finding his own scattered through the field of the world and giving everything to obtain them. The point Sirach made holds either way — hidden treasure profits no one until someone finds it, and finding it is worth everything.
cards.s_text: Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man has found, he hides, and for joy thereof goes and selleth all that he has, and buyeth that field.
cards.t_text: Wisdom that is hid, and treasure that is hoarded up, what profit is in them both?

cards.note: *A faithfull friend is a strong defence: and he that has found such an one has found a treasure.* (Ecclesiasticus 6:14). *Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls:* (Matthew 13:45). Sirach says a faithful friend is a treasure, and the next verse says nothing countervails him; there is no price you could set against him. Yahusha (Jesus) says the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking goodly pearls who finds one worth everything he owns and sells all to have it. The merchant is Yahuah (God), and the pearl is the seed of promise — always the few, scattered like gold through the dust of the earth, and worth to him everything he has. Sirach knew that kind of worth in a friend; the Father knows it in his own, and when he finds them he does not haggle.
cards.s_text: Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls:
cards.t_text: A faithfull friend is a strong defence: and he that has found such an one has found a treasure.

cards.note: *I preferred her before sceptres and thrones, and esteemed riches nothing in comparison of her.* (Wisdom of Solomon 7:8). *Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls:* (Matthew 13:45). A king with a sceptre and a throne in hand says he preferred wisdom before both of them and counted riches nothing beside her. The merchant in the parable does the same arithmetic over one pearl: he sells all he has to get it. That merchant is Yahuah (God), and the pearl of great price is the seed of promise, the few he has always called his treasure, found scattered in the nations like gold in the dust of the earth. Solomon weighed sceptres against wisdom and they came up light; the Father weighs everything against his own and pays it all.
cards.s_text: Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls:
cards.t_text: I preferred her before sceptres and thrones, and esteemed riches nothing in comparison of her.

cards.note: *For she is a treasure to men that never fails: which they that use become the friends of Yahuah (God), being commended for the gifts that come from learning.* (Wisdom of Solomon 7:14). *Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.* (Matthew 13:44). Wisdom is a treasure to men that never fails, and those who use her become the friends of Yahuah (God). The King says the kingdom of heaven is like treasure hid in a field, found by a man who hides it again, sells all he has for joy, and buys the field. The man who buys the field is Yahuah (God), and the treasure hid in it is the seed of promise, the few scattered through the field of the world like gold in the dust of the earth; he gives everything to have the field so that he has them. The one who learns wisdom becomes his friend; the one he buys the field for was his treasure before anyone dug.
cards.s_text: Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man has found, he hides, and for joy thereof goes and selleth all that he has, and buyeth that field.
cards.t_text: For she is a treasure to men that never fails: which they that use become the friends of Yahuah (God), being commended for the gifts that come from learning.

cards.note: *And the Most High shall appear upon the seat of judgment, and misery shall pass away, and the long suffering shall have an end: But judgment only shall remain, truth shall stand, and faith shall wax strong: And the work shall follow, and the reward shall be shewed, and the good deeds shall be of force, and wicked deeds shall bear no rule.* 2 Esdras (4 Ezra) 7:33-35 shows the last end of the road: the Most High upon the seat of judgment after the Messiah's reign, after the seven days of silence and the earth restoring those that are asleep in her (2 Esdras 7:28-32). Matt 13:49's *so shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just* is the severing at his coming, before the reign — the wicked taken out first, the just kept. Both are the one King's judgment, at the two edges of the reign: the severing at the end of the age, and the seat of judgment when the dead are judged.
cards.s_text: So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just,
cards.t_text: And the Most High shall appear upon the seat of judgment, and misery shall pass away, and the long suffering shall have an end:

cards.note: *There be many created, but few shall be saved.* (2 Esdras 8:3). *So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just,* (Matthew 13:49). Ezra is told that many are created but few saved, after the likeness of much clay and little gold (2 Esdras 8:2). Yahusha (Jesus) puts the sorting at the end of the world, when the angels sever the wicked from among the just as a net full of every kind is sorted on the shore. The net gathers all; the shore keeps few. The few saved are what remains when that severing is done.
cards.s_text: So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just,
cards.t_text: There be many created, but few shall be saved.

cards.note: *They shall judge the nations, and have dominion over the people, and their Elohim (God) shall reign for ever.* (Wisdom of Solomon 3:8). *So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just,* (Matthew 13:49). Wisdom says the righteous will judge the nations and have dominion over the people. Yahusha (Jesus) says what has to happen first: at the end of the age the angels come and sever the wicked from among the just. The sorting comes before the ruling. Once the wicked are taken out from among them, the just who are left are the ones Wisdom sees judging the nations — a kingdom of priests to the peoples left alive after that day, under an Elohim (God) who reigns for ever.
cards.s_text: So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just,
cards.t_text: They shall judge the nations, and have dominion over the people, and their Elohim (God) shall reign for ever.

cards.note: *Nevertheless through envy of the devil came death into the world: and they that do hold of his side do find it.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24). *The enemy that sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels.* (Matthew 13:39). Wisdom names where death came from — the envy of the devil — and who finds it: they that hold of his side. Yahusha (Jesus) names the same enemy as the one who sowed the tares in the field, and in the verse before he calls the tares the children of the wicked one. The serpent in the garden, the watchers who corrupted the earth, the sower of tares in the field — it is one enemy doing one work across the whole story. Those who are of his side come to his end, because the seed shows at the harvest.
cards.s_text: The enemy that sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels.
cards.t_text: Nevertheless through envy of the devil came death into the world: and they that do hold of his side do find it.

cards.note: *Then stood up Elias the prophet as fire, and his word burned like a lamp.* (Ecclesiasticus 48:1). *For Herod had laid hold on John, and bound him, and put him in prison for Herodias’ sake, his brother Philip’s wife.* (Matthew 14:3). Elijah's fire burned hottest at the king's court. He told Ahab to his face that the house of Ahab had forsaken the commandments of Yahuah (God), and Jezebel sought his life for it. John carried the same fire to Herod's court and said *it is not lawful for thee to have her* (Matthew 14:4), the Torah spoken against the king's own bed (Leviticus 18:16). Herod answered the prophet the way Ahab's house had answered Elijah: the king turned on him and a queen wanted him dead; this time the prophet was caught and bound. The word that burns like a lamp is not dimmed for royalty, and royalty does not forgive it.
cards.s_text: For Herod had laid hold on John, and bound him, and put him in prison for Herodias’ sake, his brother Philip’s wife.
cards.t_text: Then stood up Elias the prophet as fire, and his word burned like a lamp.

cards.note: *He brought a sore famine upon them, and by his zeal he diminished their number.* (Ecclesiasticus 48:2). *For Herod had laid hold on John, and bound him, and put him in prison for Herodias’ sake, his brother Philip’s wife.* (Matthew 14:3). Elijah's zeal against Ahab's idolatry shut up heaven; *there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word* (1 Kings 17:1), and the famine thinned the land. John's zeal against Herod's unlawful marriage brought no famine; it brought a prison cell and, before long, his head on a platter. The zeal is the same zeal, a prophet unwilling to let a king break the Torah in peace. Sirach records what it cost Ahab's people; Matthew records what it cost the prophet. Neither man softened the word to spare himself the consequences.
cards.s_text: For Herod had laid hold on John, and bound him, and put him in prison for Herodias’ sake, his brother Philip’s wife.
cards.t_text: He brought a sore famine upon them, and by his zeal he diminished their number.

cards.note: *Who were ordained for reproofs in their times, to pacify the wrath of the judgment of Yahuah (God), before it brake forth into fury, and to turn the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.* (Ecclesiasticus 48:10). *And when he would have put him to death, he feared the multitude, because they counted him as a prophet.* (Matthew 14:5). Herod would have killed John and did not, because the people counted him a prophet. They were right, and more right than they knew. Sirach describes the prophet they were looking at: ordained for reproofs in his time, to hold back the wrath of judgment before it broke out, to turn the heart of the father to the son, to restore the tribes of Jacob. John reproved a king, called a nation to turn, and prepared the way for the one who gathers Jacob. Herod feared the crowd and not the Torah, and the crowd, for once, had the better instinct.
cards.s_text: And when he would have put him to death, he feared the multitude, because they counted him as a prophet.
cards.t_text: Who were ordained for reproofs in their times, to pacify the wrath of the judgment of Yahuah (God), before it brake forth into fury, and to turn the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.

cards.note: *Blessed are they that saw you, and slept in love; for we shall surely live.* (Ecclesiasticus 48:11). *And his disciples came, and took up the body, and buried it, and went and told Yahusha (Jesus).* (Matthew 14:12). Sirach blesses the ones who saw Elijah and then fell asleep in love, and gives the reason in one line: for we shall surely live. Death is a sleep for the righteous, and the sleeper will wake. John's disciples saw the Elijah of their day, and when Herod took his head they took up his body and buried him, and then they went and told Yahusha (Jesus). They carried the news of the prophet's death to the one who holds the life Sirach was sure of. They had seen Elijah, they buried him in love, and they walked straight to the resurrection.
cards.s_text: And his disciples came, and took up the body, and buried it, and went and told Yahusha (Jesus).
cards.t_text: Blessed are they that saw you, and slept in love; for we shall surely live.

cards.note: *Then had I pity upon your mournings, and gave you manna to eat; so you did eat angels’ bread.* (2 Esdras 1:19). *When Yahusha (Jesus) heard of it, he departed thence by ship into a desert place apart: and when the people had heard thereof, they followed him on foot out of the cities.* (Matthew 14:13). In 2 Esdras Yahuah (God) reminds the people that when they murmured in the wilderness he pitied them and fed them with manna, angels' bread. In Matthew the King goes by ship into a desert place and the people follow on foot out of the cities, and the verses that follow say he was moved with compassion and fed them there. The same pity, the same wilderness, the same bread given to a multitude that had nothing. The one who fed the fathers by the hand of Moses fed the children with his own hands by the sea of Galilee.
cards.s_text: When Yahusha (Jesus) heard of it, he departed thence by ship into a desert place apart: and when the people had heard thereof, they followed him on foot out of the cities.
cards.t_text: Then had I pity upon your mournings, and gave you manna to eat; so you did eat angels’ bread.

cards.note: *Instead of which you feddest your own people with angels’ food, and did send them from heaven bread prepared without their labour, able to content every man’s delight, and agreeing to every taste.* (Wisdom of Solomon 16:20). *And he commanded the multitude to sit down on the grass, and took the five loaves, and the two fishes, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, and brake, and gave the loaves to his disciples, and the disciples to the multitude.* (Matthew 14:19). Bread from heaven, prepared without their labour, was how the Father fed his own people in the wilderness. On the grass in a desert place Yahusha (Jesus) looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and the loaves go out through the disciples' hands to a multitude that brought nothing but its hunger. The same hand that sent the manna is feeding Yashar'el (Israel) again, and John's account of this same meal ends with him saying who the bread is: *I am the bread of life* (John 6:35).
cards.s_text: And he commanded the multitude to sit down on the grass, and took the five loaves, and the two fishes, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, and brake, and gave the loaves to his disciples, and the disciples to the multitude.
cards.t_text: Instead of which you feddest your own people with angels’ food, and did send them from heaven bread prepared without their labour, able to content every man’s delight, and agreeing to every taste.

cards.note: *That your children, O Yahuah (God), whom you lovest, might know, that it is not the growing of fruits that nourishes man: but that it is your word, which preserves them that put their trust in you.* (Wisdom of Solomon 16:26). *And he commanded the multitude to sit down on the grass, and took the five loaves, and the two fishes, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, and brake, and gave the loaves to his disciples, and the disciples to the multitude.* (Matthew 14:19). The manna was a lesson, and Wisdom of Solomon says what the lesson was: it is not the harvest that keeps a man alive but the word of Yahuah (God). When the King blesses five loaves and feeds a multitude, the loaves are the smaller thing; the disciples who hand them out have been receiving his word all along, and in John's telling of this same meal he says outright that his words are spirit and life (John 6:63). The bread points past itself to the word that preserves those who trust him.
cards.s_text: And he commanded the multitude to sit down on the grass, and took the five loaves, and the two fishes, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, and brake, and gave the loaves to his disciples, and the disciples to the multitude.
cards.t_text: That your children, O Yahuah (God), whom you lovest, might know, that it is not the growing of fruits that nourishes man: but that it is your word, which preserves them that put their trust in you.

cards.note: *Come to me, all you that be desirous of me, and fill yourselves with my fruits.* (Ecclesiasticus 24:19). *And they did all eat, and were filled: and they took up of the fragments that remained twelve baskets full.* (Matthew 14:20). Wisdom says come and fill yourselves with my fruits, and in the desert place Yahusha (Jesus) did exactly that: the multitude came to him, they ate, and they were filled. He is the Wisdom of Ecclesiasticus 24 feeding her children with her own hand, and the invitation of Matthew 11:28, *come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden*, is the same mouth speaking. Twelve baskets were left over, one for every tribe of Yashar'el (Israel), and the leftover says the feeding was never meant for that hillside alone. The scattered children of Wisdom will be gathered and fed the same way.
cards.s_text: And they did all eat, and were filled: and they took up of the fragments that remained twelve baskets full.
cards.t_text: Come to me, all you that be desirous of me, and fill yourselves with my fruits.

cards.note: *By his counsel he appeaseth the deep, and planteth islands in it.* (Ecclesiasticus 43:23). *And in the fourth watch of the night Yahusha (Jesus) went unto them, walking on the sea.* (Matthew 14:25). Sirach praises the Maker who stills the deep by his counsel and sets islands in it, and Job says of the same one that he *alone spreadeth out the heavens, and treadeth upon the waves of the sea* (Job 9:8). In the fourth watch of the night the disciples watch a man do what Job said belongs to Elohim (God) alone. The one whose counsel appeases the deep is walking across it. The one who spoke the sea into its bounds came in flesh and treads on his own work.
cards.s_text: And in the fourth watch of the night Yahusha (Jesus) went unto them, walking on the sea.
cards.t_text: By his counsel he appeaseth the deep, and planteth islands in it.

cards.note: *For in it be strange and wondrous works, variety of all kinds of beasts and whales created.* (Ecclesiasticus 43:25). *And in the fourth watch of the night Yahusha (Jesus) went unto them, walking on the sea.* (Matthew 14:25). Sirach looks at the sea as a storehouse of the Creator's wonders, every beast and whale in it created, and in the next line he says *by his word all things consist* (Ecclesiasticus 43:26). The disciples saw a figure on the water and took it for a spirit. What they saw was the Creator of the sea walking on his own creation, and when he spoke he gave them his name, *it is I; be not afraid* (Matthew 14:27). The word that holds the sea together was the word speaking to them from on top of it.
cards.s_text: And in the fourth watch of the night Yahusha (Jesus) went unto them, walking on the sea.
cards.t_text: For in it be strange and wondrous works, variety of all kinds of beasts and whales created.

cards.note: *But your providence, O Father, governeth it: for you have made a way in the sea, and a safe path in the waves;* (Wisdom of Solomon 14:3). *And in the fourth watch of the night Yahusha (Jesus) went unto them, walking on the sea.* (Matthew 14:25). The Father has made a way in the sea and a safe path in the waves; the psalmist says the same, that his way is in the sea and his path in the great waters (Psalm 77:19). In the fourth watch the King walks that way, on the water, toward a boat full of men being tossed by it. The Formed one walks the path the Father's providence made, and when Peter steps out and sinks, the hand that catches him (Matthew 14:31) is the safe path in the waves Solomon prayed about. The way in the sea was never a figure of speech; a man walked it.
cards.s_text: And in the fourth watch of the night Yahusha (Jesus) went unto them, walking on the sea.
cards.t_text: But your providence, O Father, governeth it: for you have made a way in the sea, and a safe path in the waves;

cards.note: *Your Almighty word leaped down from heaven out of your royal throne, as a fierce man of war into the midst of a land of destruction,* (Wisdom of Solomon 18:15). *But straightway Yahusha (Jesus) spake unto them, saying, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.* (Matthew 14:27). The almighty word leaped down from the throne into Egypt's night as a man of war. In the fourth watch of another night the disciples see a figure on the sea and are terrified, and the Word speaks: it is I; be not afraid. The one who came down from the Father's throne on Passover night is the same one walking the dark water, the Word who was with Elohim (God) and was made flesh (John 1:1, 14). Wisdom of Solomon shows the Word as one who comes down and acts; Matthew shows him in flesh naming himself.
cards.s_text: But straightway Yahusha (Jesus) spake unto them, saying, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.
cards.t_text: Your Almighty word leaped down from heaven out of your royal throne, as a fierce man of war into the midst of a land of destruction,

cards.note: *I came out of the mouth of the Most High, and covered the earth as a cloud.* (Ecclesiasticus 24:3). *But straightway Yahusha (Jesus) spake unto them, saying, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.* (Matthew 14:27). Wisdom says she came out of the mouth of the Most High and covered the earth as a cloud. The one who came out of the Father's mouth is the Word the Father spoke — the Formed one beside the formless Maker — and the prophets knew him as the one who rides the clouds. On the water Yahusha (Jesus) says to the frightened men, it is I, the same words he uses when he says that before Abraham was, I am. The Wisdom that came out of the mouth of the Most High is the one walking on the sea, and he tells them not to be afraid.
cards.s_text: But straightway Yahusha (Jesus) spake unto them, saying, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.
cards.t_text: I came out of the mouth of the Most High, and covered the earth as a cloud.

cards.note: *O Yahuah (God) of my fathers, and Yahuah (God) of mercy, who have made all things with your word,* (Wisdom of Solomon 9:1). *But straightway Yahusha (Jesus) spake unto them, saying, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.* (Matthew 14:27). Solomon prays to the Elohim (God) of his fathers who made all things with his word. John says the same of the Word: all things were made by him, and without him was not any thing made that was made (John 1:3). In the fourth watch the disciples see a figure walking on the sea and cry out, and he answers with the name the Formed one spoke from the bush: it is I, be not afraid. The one walking on the water is the Word the sea was made with, come in flesh and standing on his own handiwork. The Father made all things with his word; here the word is walking toward the boat.
cards.s_text: But straightway Yahusha (Jesus) spake unto them, saying, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.
cards.t_text: O Yahuah (God) of my fathers, and Yahuah (God) of mercy, who have made all things with your word,

cards.note: *Therefore let us lie in wait for the righteous; because he is not for our turn, and he is clean contrary to our doings: he upbraideth us with our offending the law, and objecteth to our infamy the transgressings of our education.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:12). *For Herod had laid hold on John, and bound him, and put him in prison for Herodias’ sake, his brother Philip’s wife.* (Matthew 14:3). John upbraided Herod with his offending the law, *it is not lawful for thee to have her* (Matthew 14:4), and Herod laid hold on him and bound him. That is Wisdom of Solomon 2:12 acted out at a king's court: the righteous one is clean contrary to what the king is doing, his word reproves the king's bed, and so the king and the woman lie in wait for him. The same reflex shows up wherever a righteous man reproves a system that has left the Torah, in the Pharisees who take counsel to destroy Yahusha (Jesus) (Matthew 12:14) and in the chief priests who do the same (Matthew 26:3–4). Herod is one more instance of a very old disposition.
cards.s_text: For Herod had laid hold on John, and bound him, and put him in prison for Herodias’ sake, his brother Philip’s wife.
cards.t_text: Therefore let us lie in wait for the righteous; because he is not for our turn, and he is clean contrary to our doings: he upbraideth us with our offending the law, and objecteth to our infamy the transgressings of our education.

cards.note: *Let us examine him with despitefulness and torture, that we may know his meekness, and prove his patience.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:19). *And when he would have put him to death, he feared the multitude, because they counted him as a prophet.* (Matthew 14:5). Wisdom shows the heart of the ungodly toward the righteous: torment him and see how long his meekness holds. Herod carried that heart toward John; he would have put him to death already, and only his fear of the crowd held his hand. The restraint was politics, not mercy, and a birthday oath later removed it. Isaiah's sheep dumb before her shearers, John in Herod's prison, Yahusha (Jesus) before Pilate — the ungodly keep running the same test on the righteous, and the righteous keep answering it the same way.
cards.s_text: And when he would have put him to death, he feared the multitude, because they counted him as a prophet.
cards.t_text: Let us examine him with despitefulness and torture, that we may know his meekness, and prove his patience.

cards.note: *Let us condemn him with a shameful death: for by his own saying he shall be respected.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:20). *And he sent, and beheaded John in the prison.* (Matthew 14:10). A shameful death is not the honored end of a long life; it is a death arranged by men who want the righteous man gone. John's beheading in Herod's prison, on the strength of a rash birthday oath, is exactly the death Wisdom describes. The ungodly did not wait for the Father's verdict on his words; they gave their own. The prophets who upbraided the nation with the Torah died this way before him, and the King tells that whole history over in Matthew 23.
cards.s_text: And he sent, and beheaded John in the prison.
cards.t_text: Let us condemn him with a shameful death: for by his own saying he shall be respected.

cards.note: *Hear me your father, O children, and do thereafter, that you may be safe.* (Ecclesiasticus 3:1). *For Elohim (God) commanded, saying, Honour thy father and mother: and, He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death.* (Matthew 15:4). Sirach begins his teaching on parents by speaking as a father: hear me, children, and do what I say, so that you may be safe. The whole chapter rests on the fifth commandment, the one Yahusha (Jesus) quotes back to the Pharisees in Matthew 15:4, honour thy father and mother, with the death penalty for cursing them attached. The tradition he is exposing in the verses that follow let a man vow to the altar what his aged parents needed and call himself free of them. Sirach had tied the children's safety to hearing and doing their father's word; the tradition untied it, and the Messiah names what Elohim (God) commanded to tie it back.
cards.s_text: For Elohim (God) commanded, saying, Honour your father and mother: and, He that curses father or mother, let him die the death.
cards.t_text: Hear me your father, O children, and do thereafter, that you may be safe.

cards.note: *Honour your father and mother both in word and deed, that a blessing may come upon you from them.* (Ecclesiasticus 3:8). *For Elohim (God) commanded, saying, Honour thy father and mother: and, He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death.* (Matthew 15:4). Honour your parents both in word and deed, Sirach says, and the two words are the whole argument. The corban tradition Yahusha (Jesus) exposes in Matthew 15 kept the word and dropped the deed: a man could speak a vow that sounded devout while the support his father and mother needed was cut off by it. The Messiah answers with what Elohim (God) commanded, honour thy father and mother, with no room left for honour that is spoken and not done. Sirach had closed that gap generations before by naming both halves, and a tradition that keeps one half has kept neither.
cards.s_text: For Elohim (God) commanded, saying, Honour your father and mother: and, He that curses father or mother, let him die the death.
cards.t_text: Honour your father and mother both in word and deed, that a blessing may come upon you from them.

cards.note: *Honour your father with your whole heart, and forget not the sorrows of your mother.* (Ecclesiasticus 7:27). *For Elohim (God) commanded, saying, Honour thy father and mother: and, He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death.* (Matthew 15:4). Sirach says honour your father with your whole heart, and he adds the mother's sorrows so the son remembers what he cost her. Matthew 15:4 is the commandment behind it, honour thy father and mother, quoted by Yahusha (Jesus) against a tradition that let a son divide his heart, a vow to the altar in one half and nothing left for his parents in the other. Whole heart is Sirach's word against that division. Later in the same chapter the Messiah says what defiles comes out of the heart (vv.18–20), and the corban device is the proof: an honour split by a vow was defiled before the vow was spoken.
cards.s_text: For Elohim (God) commanded, saying, Honour your father and mother: and, He that curses father or mother, let him die the death.
cards.t_text: Honour your father with your whole heart, and forget not the sorrows of your mother.

cards.note: *He that forsaketh his father is as a blasphemer; and he that angereth his mother is cursed: of Yahuah (God).* (Ecclesiasticus 3:16). *And honour not his father or his mother, he shall be free. Thus have ye made the commandment of Elohim (God) of none effect by your tradition.* (Matthew 15:6). Sirach does not treat neglect of parents as a small fault. To forsake a father is as blasphemy; to anger a mother is to be cursed of Yahuah (God). That is the weight behind Matthew 15:6, where a tradition lets a son honour not his father or his mother and call himself free, and the Messiah says the commandment of Elohim (God) has been made of none effect. What the tradition filed under devotion, Sirach had filed under blasphemy and curse. Yahusha (Jesus) is not inventing a harsher reading; he is reading the commandment the way the fathers already read it.
cards.s_text: And honour not his father or his mother, he shall be free. Thus have you made the commandment of Elohim (God) of none effect by your tradition.
cards.t_text: He that forsaketh his father is as a blasphemer; and he that angereth his mother is cursed: of Yahuah (God).

cards.note: *And when he had called him, he said, My son, when I am dead, bury me; and despise not your mother, but honour her all the days of your life, and do that which shall please her, and grieve her not.* (Tobit 4:3). *For Elohim (God) commanded, saying, Honour thy father and mother: and, He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death.* (Matthew 15:4). A dying father in exile tells his son: honour your mother all the days of her life, please her, grieve her not. That is the fifth commandment lived out to the end of a parent's days, in a household far from the land. Yahusha (Jesus) quotes the same commandment against a tradition that let a man say *It is a gift* and so be freed from supporting his parents (15:5–6). Tobit shows what the commandment looks like when it is kept; the tradition shows what it looks like when a religious system finds a way around it, and it is the system that is being answered, not the people who were taught it.
cards.s_text: For Elohim (God) commanded, saying, Honour your father and mother: and, He that curses father or mother, let him die the death.
cards.t_text: And when he had called him, he said, My son, when I am dead, bury me; and despise not your mother, but honour her all the days of your life, and do that which shall please her, and grieve her not.

cards.note: *Say not you, It is through Yahuah (God) that I fell away: for you oughtest not to do the things that he hates.* (Ecclesiasticus 15:11). *Not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man; but that which cometh out of the mouth, this defileth a man.* (Matthew 15:11). Sirach forbids a man to say he fell away through Yahuah (God); the things he hates are not his doing. Yahusha (Jesus) says defilement does not come in through the mouth but out of it — the source is the man's own heart. The two verses fence off the same lie from opposite sides: the Father does not cause the falling, and bread eaten with unwashed hands does not cause the defilement. What a man does and says comes from inside him, and that is where the Torah has always located it.
cards.s_text: Not that which goes into the mouth defiles a man; but that which comes out of the mouth, this defiles a man.
cards.t_text: Say not you, It is through Yahuah (God) that I fell away: for you oughtest not to do the things that he hates.

cards.note: *He has commanded no man to do wickedly, neither has he given any man licence to sin.* (Ecclesiasticus 15:20). *But those things which proceed out of the mouth come forth from the heart; and they defile the man.* (Matthew 15:18). Sirach says plainly that Yahuah (God) has commanded no man to do wickedly and given no man licence to sin. Yahusha (Jesus) says what defiles a man comes out of his own heart. Put the two together and the source of sin is found — not the Father, not the bread, not the unwashed hands the Pharisees fussed over, but the heart. Any teaching that gives licence to sin is giving what Yahuah (God) never gave.
cards.s_text: But those things which proceed out of the mouth come forth from the heart; and they defile the man.
cards.t_text: He has commanded no man to do wickedly, neither has he given any man licence to sin.

cards.note: *The fruit declareth if the tree have been dressed; so is the utterance of a conceit in the heart of man.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:6). *But those things which proceed out of the mouth come forth from the heart; and they defile the man.* (Matthew 15:18). The fruit shows the tree, Sirach says, and a man's speech shows what his heart has conceived. Yahusha (Jesus) says the same when the Pharisees fuss over unwashed hands: what defiles a man comes out of his mouth, and it comes from the heart. The heart is the source. Bread eaten with unwashed hands does not defile the man; what defiles him is what his own heart conceives and his mouth lets out, and the good tree bringing forth good fruit in Matthew 7:17 is the same picture. Watch what comes out, and you have seen what is inside.
cards.s_text: But those things which proceed out of the mouth come forth from the heart; and they defile the man.
cards.t_text: The fruit declareth if the tree have been dressed; so is the utterance of a conceit in the heart of man.

cards.note: *Therefore beware of murmuring, which is unprofitable; and refrain your tongue from backbiting: for there is no word so secret, that shall go for nought: and the mouth that belieth slayeth the soul.* (Wisdom of Solomon 1:11). *For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies:* (Matthew 15:19). Wisdom of Solomon warns about the mouth: murmuring, backbiting, the lying mouth that kills the soul. Yahusha (Jesus) traces the mouth back to its source, *those things which proceed out of the mouth come forth from the heart* (Matthew 15:18), and then lists what comes out of it, false witness and blasphemies among them. The two lists overlap because they are describing one thing from two ends: the heart is where the evil starts, and the tongue is where it shows. That is why the promise of the new covenant is a heart with the Torah written on it (Jeremiah 31:33), because a clean mouth needs a clean spring.
cards.s_text: For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies:
cards.t_text: Therefore beware of murmuring, which is unprofitable; and refrain your tongue from backbiting: for there is no word so secret, that shall go for nought: and the mouth that belieth slayeth the soul.

cards.note: *Have mercy upon us, O Yahuah (God) of all, and behold us:* (Ecclesiasticus 36:1). *But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel).* (Matthew 15:24). Sirach opens his great prayer with a cry for mercy to the Elohim (God) of all, and the prayer goes on to ask that all the tribes of Jacob be gathered and inherited as from the beginning. Yahusha (Jesus) says he was not sent but to the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel). The one being asked for mercy in Sirach's prayer is the one who answered it in person, sent to the very scattered house the prayer was about. Behold us, Sirach prays; the Shepherd came looking for the sheep.
cards.s_text: But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel).
cards.t_text: Have mercy upon us, O Yahuah (God) of all, and behold us:

cards.note: *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning.* (Ecclesiasticus 36:11). *But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel).* (Matthew 15:24). Sirach prays for the gathering of all the tribes of Jacob, back into the inheritance as from the beginning. Yahusha (Jesus) says he was sent to the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel). The prayer and the mission have the same object: not Yahudah (Judah) alone, who had a temple and a land, but the whole house that had been scattered and lost among the nations. The prophets promised it, Sirach prayed it, and the King came for it.
cards.s_text: But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel).
cards.t_text: Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning.

cards.note: *Those are the ten tribes, which were carried away prisoners out of their own land in the time of Osea the king, whom Salmanasar the king of Assyria led away captive, and he carried them over the waters, and so came they into another land.* (2 Esdras 13:40). *But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel).* (Matthew 15:24). When the woman of Canaan pressed him, Yahusha (Jesus) named the scope of his sending: the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel) — and she, who heard the Shepherd and would not be turned away, was one of them. Ezra had already been shown who that house is, the ten tribes Shalmaneser led away captive over the waters into another land, who never returned. The lost sheep were not a figure of speech; they were a people with a date, a captor, and a direction of travel, the same carrying away the book of Kings records (2 Kings 17:6). The King was sent to them, and the prophets who promised their gathering (Jeremiah 31; Ezekiel 37) were speaking of the same people.
cards.s_text: But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel).
cards.t_text: Those are the ten tribes, which were carried away prisoners out of their own land in the time of Osea the king, whom Salmanasar the king of Assyria led away captive, and he carried them over the waters, and so came they into another land.

cards.note: *But those that be left behind of your people are they that are found within my borders.* (2 Esdras 13:48). *But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel).* (Matthew 15:24). The vision does not forget the ones who never left. After the ten tribes come home, Ezra is told that those left behind of his people are the ones found within the borders of the land, the remnant of Yahudah (Judah) that stayed. When Yahusha (Jesus) says he was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel), his sending reaches both of these: the multitudes of Galilee and Yahudah (Judah) he walked among inside the borders, and the scattered house beyond the waters his apostles would be sent after. The house of Yashar'el (Israel) is both of them, the ones who stayed and the ones who were carried, and the King's mission is to the whole house.
cards.s_text: But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel).
cards.t_text: But those that be left behind of your people are they that are found within my borders.

cards.note: *And he will scourge us for our iniquities, and will have mercy again, and will gather us out of all nations, among whom he has scattered us.* (Tobit 13:5). *But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel).* (Matthew 15:24). Tobit names who gets gathered and from where: the people Yahuah (God) scourged and scattered, brought back out of all the nations. Ezekiel had said the same, *I will take the children of Yashar'el (Israel) from among the heathen, whither they be gone, and will gather them on every side* (Ezekiel 37:21). When Yahusha (Jesus) says he is not sent but to the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel), he is stating the scope of that gathering, not narrowing his mercy. He said it to the woman of Canaan, and she was not turned away; the sheep hear the Shepherd's voice wherever the scattering has carried them, and the hearing shows who they are. The mission to the lost sheep is the mercy Tobit said would follow the scourge.
cards.s_text: But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel).
cards.t_text: And he will scourge us for our iniquities, and will have mercy again, and will gather us out of all nations, among whom he has scattered us.

cards.note: *For if the just man be the son of Yahuah (God), he will help him, and deliver him from the hand of his enemies.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:18). *And Simon Peter answered and said, Thou art the Messiah (Christ), the Son of the living Elohim (God).* (Matthew 16:16). The same words come from two mouths. The ungodly in Wisdom say it in mockery — if the just man is the son of Yahuah (God), let him be delivered. Peter says it in confession — thou art the Messiah (Christ), the Son of the living Elohim (God). What the wicked used as a taunt against the righteous man is the title the Father reveals to Peter at the turning point of the gospel. The just man of Wisdom is the Son Peter confessed, and the plot to test him never changed who he was.
cards.s_text: And Simon Peter answered and said, You are the Messiah (Christ), the Son of the living Elohim (God).
cards.t_text: For if the just man be the son of Yahuah (God), he will help him, and deliver him from the hand of his enemies.

cards.note: *Therefore let us lie in wait for the righteous; because he is not for our turn, and he is clean contrary to our doings: he upbraideth us with our offending the law, and objecteth to our infamy the transgressings of our education.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:12). *From that time forth began Yahusha (Jesus) to shew unto his disciples, how that he must go unto Jerusalem, and suffer many things of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and be raised again the third day.* (Matthew 16:21). The ungodly in Wisdom of Solomon 2 begin by lying in wait and end by resolving, *let us condemn him with a shameful death* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:20). Yahusha (Jesus) tells his disciples the same ending in advance, suffering at the hands of the elders, chief priests and scribes, and death in Jerusalem. The religious leadership of the day fills the role Wisdom wrote for the ungodly, a system that could not bear a righteous man whose life reproved it. But he adds a line Wisdom's plotters never saw coming, raised again the third day, and Wisdom itself knew it: the souls of the righteous are in the hand of Elohim (God) (Wisdom of Solomon 3:1).
cards.s_text: From that time forth began Yahusha (Jesus) to shew unto his disciples, how that he must go unto Jerusalem, and suffer many things of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and be raised again the third day.
cards.t_text: Therefore let us lie in wait for the righteous; because he is not for our turn, and he is clean contrary to our doings: he upbraideth us with our offending the law, and objecteth to our infamy the transgressings of our education.

cards.note: *We are esteemed of him as counterfeits: he abstaineth from our ways as from filthiness: he pronounceth the end of the just to be blessed, and makes his boast that Yahuah (God) is his father.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:16). *From that time forth began Yahusha (Jesus) to shew unto his disciples, how that he must go unto Jerusalem, and suffer many things of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and be raised again the third day.* (Matthew 16:21). The men who esteemed themselves righteous felt judged by a man who would not walk their way and who called Yahuah (God) his father. Wisdom puts the grievance in their own mouths; Matthew names who held it in Yahusha's (Jesus') day — the elders, the chief priests and the scribes, the men who held the seats of religion in Jerusalem. He told his disciples plainly that he must suffer at their hands and be killed, because a life that counts their ways as filthiness is an indictment they could not leave standing. It was the seat of the system that rose against him, not the people sitting under it.
cards.s_text: From that time forth began Yahusha (Jesus) to shew unto his disciples, how that he must go unto Jerusalem, and suffer many things of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and be raised again the third day.
cards.t_text: We are esteemed of him as counterfeits: he abstaineth from our ways as from filthiness: he pronounceth the end of the just to be blessed, and makes his boast that Yahuah (God) is his father.

cards.note: *Let us condemn him with a shameful death: for by his own saying he shall be respected.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:20). *From that time forth began Yahusha (Jesus) to shew unto his disciples, how that he must go unto Jerusalem, and suffer many things of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and be raised again the third day.* (Matthew 16:21). Wisdom says the ungodly will condemn the righteous man to a shameful death. Yahusha (Jesus) tells his disciples he must suffer and be killed, and later he names how: delivered to be mocked, scourged and crucified (Matthew 20:19). The cross was the shameful death — the Torah itself says *he that is hanged is accursed of Elohim (God)* (Deuteronomy 21:23), so the men who hung him there meant it as the Father's own rejection of him. Isaiah's servant, Wisdom's just man and the passion the King announced all meet at that tree. And he named the third day in the same breath, which is the answer to the whole plot.
cards.s_text: From that time forth began Yahusha (Jesus) to shew unto his disciples, how that he must go unto Jerusalem, and suffer many things of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and be raised again the third day.
cards.t_text: Let us condemn him with a shameful death: for by his own saying he shall be respected.

cards.note: *But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of Yahuah (God), and there shall no torment touch them.* (Wisdom of Solomon 3:1). *From that time forth began Yahusha (Jesus) to shew unto his disciples, how that he must go unto Jerusalem, and suffer many things of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and be raised again the third day.* (Matthew 16:21). Wisdom 2 ends with the just man condemned to a shameful death; Wisdom 3 opens with his soul in the hand of Yahuah (God), untouched by torment. Yahusha (Jesus) tells his disciples both halves in one sentence — he must be killed, and be raised again the third day. The being killed is the shameful death; the being raised is the hand of the Father. Wisdom had already laid the two chapters side by side, and the gospel shows the one man who walked through both.
cards.s_text: From that time forth began Yahusha (Jesus) to shew unto his disciples, how that he must go unto Jerusalem, and suffer many things of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and be raised again the third day.
cards.t_text: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of Yahuah (God), and there shall no torment touch them.

cards.note: *Then shall the righteous man stand in great boldness before the face of such as have afflicted him, and made no account of his labours.* (Wisdom of Solomon 5:1). *From that time forth began Yahusha (Jesus) to shew unto his disciples, how that he must go unto Jerusalem, and suffer many things of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and be raised again the third day.* (Matthew 16:21). Here the King lays out both halves at once: he will suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, be killed, and be raised the third day. Solomon saw the second half from far off, the righteous man standing in boldness before the very men who afflicted him and made no account of his labours. The third day is where that standing begins, and the King finishes the thought a few verses later, when the Son of Adam comes in the glory of his Father to reward every man according to his works (Matthew 16:27). The vindication does not make him righteous; it shows in public what was true all along.
cards.s_text: From that time forth began Yahusha (Jesus) to shew unto his disciples, how that he must go unto Jerusalem, and suffer many things of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and be raised again the third day.
cards.t_text: Then shall the righteous man stand in great boldness before the face of such as have afflicted him, and made no account of his labours.

cards.note: *For Yahuah (God) made not death: neither has he pleasure in the destruction of the living.* (Wisdom of Solomon 1:13). *And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.* (Matthew 16:18). Wisdom of Solomon says it flatly: Yahuah (God) did not make death. It came in through the envy of the devil (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24) and through the sin in the garden; it is an intruder in his creation, not his design. That is why Yahusha (Jesus) can say the gates of hell, the gates of the grave, will not prevail against the assembly he builds. A thing the Father did not make has no permanent claim on what he did make. The grave's gates held every son of Adam until the one who said this walked out through them on the third day, and because he did, the gates will not hold his people either.
cards.s_text: And I say also unto you, That you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
cards.t_text: For Yahuah (God) made not death: neither has he pleasure in the destruction of the living.

cards.note: *For you have power of life and death: you leadest to the gates of hell, and bringest up again.* (Wisdom of Solomon 16:13). *And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.* (Matthew 16:18). The gates of hell have no final say, because the one who leads down to those gates is the same one who brings up again. That is what stands behind the promise to Peter: the assembly is built on the King who would be raised the third day (he says so plainly at verse 21), and the gates that closed on him could not hold him, so they will not prevail against what he builds. The same chapter opens with the sign of Jonah (verse 4); the whole chapter is carrying this one truth, that the grave is a door the Father opens.
cards.s_text: And I say also unto you, That you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
cards.t_text: For you have power of life and death: you leadest to the gates of hell, and bringest up again.

cards.note: *Did not the souls also of the righteous ask question of these things in their chambers, saying, How long shall I hope on this fashion? when comes the fruit of the floor of our reward?* (2 Esdras 4:35). *And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.* (Matthew 16:18). The righteous dead are in chambers, Esdras is told, asking when the floor of their reward will come. They are not in torment and they are not in heaven; they are resting and waiting, and later in the book the chambers deliver up the souls committed to them at the resurrection (2 Esdras 7:32). That is what the King means when he says the gates of hell shall not prevail against his assembly. Sheol is a holding place with gates, and the gates do not hold his people past the day he calls them out. The chambers keep the righteous; they do not keep them forever.
cards.s_text: And I say also unto you, That you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
cards.t_text: Did not the souls also of the righteous ask question of these things in their chambers, saying, How long shall I hope on this fashion? when comes the fruit of the floor of our reward?

cards.note: *As his mercy is great, so is his correction also: he judges a man according to his works* (Ecclesiasticus 16:12). *For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.* (Matthew 16:27). Sirach holds mercy and correction in the same hand and says the measure of both is a man's works. Yahusha (Jesus) says the same about his own coming in his Father's glory: every man rewarded according to his works. Grace is the door home, not the cancelling of the reckoning. The judgment weighs the fruit, and the fruit comes from a heart that either received the new heart Ezekiel promised or did not.
cards.s_text: For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.
cards.t_text: As his mercy is great, so is his correction also: he judges a man according to his works

cards.note: *Make way for every work of mercy: for every man shall find according to his works.* (Ecclesiasticus 16:14). *For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.* (Matthew 16:27). Sirach ties the two halves together: make way for every work of mercy, because every man shall find according to his works. Yahusha (Jesus) says the finding happens when the Son of Adam comes in his Father's glory. Mercy done now is what is found then. The door home is opened by grace; what is weighed at the judgment is what the one who came home did after he walked in.
cards.s_text: For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.
cards.t_text: Make way for every work of mercy: for every man shall find according to his works.

cards.note: *Till he have rendered to every man according to his deeds, and to the works of men according to their devices; till he have judged the cause of his people, and made them to rejoice in his mercy.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:19). *For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.* (Matthew 16:27). Sirach says Yahuah (God) will not rest until he has rendered to every man according to his deeds and judged the cause of his people and made them rejoice in his mercy. Yahusha (Jesus) says the Son of Adam will come in the glory of his Father and reward every man according to his works. The two halves Sirach holds together are the two halves the King names: a reckoning by works for every man, and vindication and joy for his own people. Reward comes at his coming and it comes by deeds, and those who are his rejoice in mercy on that day rather than in a reckoning they skipped.
cards.s_text: For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.
cards.t_text: Till he have rendered to every man according to his deeds, and to the works of men according to their devices; till he have judged the cause of his people, and made them to rejoice in his mercy.

cards.note: *And the earth shall restore those that are asleep in her, and so shall the dust those that dwell in silence, and the secret places shall deliver those souls that were committed to them.* (2 Esdras 7:32). *For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.* (Matthew 16:27). Ezra is shown the order: first the earth gives back those asleep in her and the secret places deliver the souls committed to them, then the Most High appears on the seat of judgment, and the work follows and the reward is shown (2 Esdras 7:33–35). Yahusha (Jesus) gives the same order in one sentence: the Son of Adam comes in his Father's glory, and then he rewards every man according to his works. Resurrection first, then the reward by works. The righteous who sleep are not being rewarded somewhere now; they rest in the places committed to them until the earth restores them, and the reckoning comes after.
cards.s_text: For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.
cards.t_text: And the earth shall restore those that are asleep in her, and so shall the dust those that dwell in silence, and the secret places shall deliver those souls that were committed to them.

cards.note: *And the work shall follow, and the reward shall be shewed, and the good deeds shall be of force, and wicked deeds shall bear no rule.* (2 Esdras 7:35). *For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.* (Matthew 16:27). Ezra is told what follows the judgment seat: the work follows the man, the reward is shown, and good deeds are of force while wicked deeds bear no rule. Yahusha (Jesus) says it as plainly: when the Son of Adam comes in his Father's glory, he rewards every man according to his works. This is not a man earning his place; it is a man's deeds going with him into the day and being weighed there. The works that follow are the fruit of a heart that kept what it was given, and those with no such fruit are told to depart (Matthew 7:23).
cards.s_text: For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.
cards.t_text: And the work shall follow, and the reward shall be shewed, and the good deeds shall be of force, and wicked deeds shall bear no rule.

cards.note: *Admonish a friend, it may be he has not done it: and if he have done it, that he do it no more.* (Ecclesiasticus 19:13). *Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.* (Matthew 18:15). Sirach's counsel is to go to the friend first, because he may not have done it at all, and if he has, so that he will do it no more. Yahusha (Jesus) makes that the first step when a brother trespasses: go to him alone, tell him his fault, and if he hears you the brother is gained. Both aim at restoration, not at shame or gossip — the private word comes before anything else, and the Torah had already told a man to rebuke his neighbour rather than carry a grudge against him in his heart.
cards.s_text: Moreover if your brother shall trespass against you, go and tell him his fault between you and him alone: if he shall hear you, you have gained your brother.
cards.t_text: Admonish a friend, it may be he has not done it: and if he have done it, that he do it no more.

cards.note: *Admonish your neighbour before you threaten him; and not being angry, give place to the law of the Most High.* (Ecclesiasticus 19:17). *Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.* (Matthew 18:15). Sirach sets the order and the temper together: admonish before you threaten, and do it without anger, letting the law of the Most High govern the matter rather than your own heat. That is the spirit of the first step Yahusha (Jesus) gives — go to the brother alone and tell him his fault, which is admonition, not threat. The goal is to gain the brother, and a man cannot gain his brother while he is angry at him. The rebuke works when the Torah, not the rebuker's temper, is what it stands on.
cards.s_text: Moreover if your brother shall trespass against you, go and tell him his fault between you and him alone: if he shall hear you, you have gained your brother.
cards.t_text: Admonish your neighbour before you threaten him; and not being angry, give place to the law of the Most High.

cards.note: *Admonish a friend: for many times it is a slander, and believe not every tale.* (Ecclesiasticus 19:15). *But if he will not hear thee, then take with thee one or two more, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.* (Matthew 18:16). Sirach warns that many a report is slander and that not every tale should be believed — so go and admonish the friend rather than take the story as settled. Yahusha (Jesus) builds the same safeguard into the second step: if the brother will not hear, bring one or two more, so that every word is established in the mouth of two or three witnesses. The witnesses protect the accused from a false charge and the accuser from his own inflated one. What Sirach counseled as wisdom, the King set as procedure, and both rest on the Torah's rule that one witness is never enough.
cards.s_text: But if he will not hear you, then take with you one or two more, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.
cards.t_text: Admonish a friend: for many times it is a slander, and believe not every tale.

cards.note: *It is much better to reprove, than to be angry secretly: and he that confesseth his fault shall be preserved from hurt.* (Ecclesiasticus 20:2). *And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.* (Matthew 18:17). Sirach says open reproof is far better than secret anger, and the man who confesses his fault when reproved is preserved from hurt. That is what the third step in Matthew is for: when the private word and the witnesses have both been refused, the matter is told to the assembly in the open, where it can still be confessed and the brother still preserved. Secret anger restores no one. Open reproof, met with confession, does — and only when even the assembly is refused does the brother put himself outside.
cards.s_text: And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto you as an heathen man and a publican.
cards.t_text: It is much better to reprove, than to be angry secretly: and he that confesseth his fault shall be preserved from hurt.

cards.note: *Malice and wrath, even these are abominations; and the sinful man shall have them both.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:30). *Then came Peter to him, and said, Adonai (Lord), how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?* (Matthew 18:21). Sirach calls malice and wrath abominations, the portion of the sinful man. Peter comes to Yahusha (Jesus) still counting, asking how many times he has to forgive his brother, seven? A man who is counting offences is still holding them, and what he is holding is the malice Sirach names. The King's answer pushes past the count altogether, because the heart he is forming in his disciples is the new heart of Ezekiel 36:26, the one the Spirit moves to walk in the statutes, and that heart does not keep a tally against a brother.
cards.s_text: Then came Peter to him, and said, Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?
cards.t_text: Malice and wrath, even these are abominations; and the sinful man shall have them both.

cards.note: *Forgive your neighbour the hurt that he has done to you, so shall your sins also be forgiven when you prayest.* (Ecclesiasticus 28:2). *Yahusha (Jesus) saith unto him, I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.* (Matthew 18:22). Sirach says forgive your neighbour, and your own sins will be forgiven when you pray. Peter asks how many times, and Yahusha (Jesus) answers seventy times seven, then tells the parable of the servant who was forgiven a fortune and would not forgive a few pence, and closes it with the warning that the heavenly Father will do the same to anyone who does not forgive his brother from the heart. The Lord's Prayer had already made the same condition, forgive and be forgiven, forgive not and be not forgiven (Matthew 6:14–15). Sirach said it in one line; the King said it in a prayer, a number, and a story, and it is one teaching.
cards.s_text: Yahusha (Jesus) says unto him, I say not unto you, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.
cards.t_text: Forgive your neighbour the hurt that he has done to you, so shall your sins also be forgiven when you prayest.

cards.note: *One man bears hatred against another, and does he seek pardon from Yahuah (God)?* (Ecclesiasticus 28:3). *Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?* (Matthew 18:33). Sirach asks the plain question: a man holds hatred against another man, and he goes looking for pardon from Yahuah (God)? The parable in Matthew 18 puts that man in a story. He has just been forgiven everything he owed, and he takes his fellow servant by the throat over a trifle, and his lord asks him the very question Sirach asked, should you not have had compassion as I had pity on you? The pardon he had received was taken back. Mercy received has to become mercy given, or it does not stay.
cards.s_text: Should not you also have had compassion on your fellowservant, even as I had pity on you?
cards.t_text: One man bears hatred against another, and does he seek pardon from Yahuah (God)?

cards.note: *Remember the commandments, and bear no malice to your neighbour: remember the covenant of the Highest, and wink at ignorance.* (Ecclesiasticus 28:7). *So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses.* (Matthew 18:35). Sirach says two things in one line and means them as one: remember the commandments, and bear no malice to your neighbour; remember the covenant of the Highest, and overlook ignorance. Yahusha (Jesus) ends the parable of the unforgiving servant on the same note, that the heavenly Father will deal the same way with anyone who does not forgive his brother from the heart. Remembering the Torah and forgiving the brother are not two different religions; the law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33) is what produces a heart without malice. And the parable is plain that the forgiveness a man received can be taken back if he will not extend it; the door home stays a door, and the man who bears malice against his brother has walked away from it.
cards.s_text: So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if you from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses.
cards.t_text: Remember the commandments, and bear no malice to your neighbour: remember the covenant of the Highest, and wink at ignorance.

cards.note: *The greater you are, the more humble thyself, and you shall find favour before Yahuah (God).* (Ecclesiasticus 3:18). *And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.* (Matthew 18:3). The greater you are, the more humble yourself, Sirach says, and Yahusha (Jesus) makes it the condition of entry: except you be converted and become as little children, you do not enter the kingdom at all. The disciples had just asked who is greatest, and the answer turned their measure upside down, because in the kingdom greatness is measured by how low a man will go, not how high he is set. Sirach was teaching it at a father's table long before the disciples argued about it on the road. The one who humbles himself as a little child is the greatest in that kingdom, which is exactly the favour Sirach said the humble find.
cards.s_text: And said, Verily I say unto you, Except you be converted, and become as little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.
cards.t_text: The greater you are, the more humble thyself, and you shall find favour before Yahuah (God).

cards.note: *Yahuah (God) has cast down the thrones of proud princes, and set up the meek in their stead.* (Ecclesiasticus 10:14). *Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this little child, the same is greatest in the kingdom of heaven.* (Matthew 18:4). Sirach says Yahuah (God) has already done it: the proud cast off their thrones, the meek set in their place. Yahusha (Jesus) says the one who humbles himself as a little child is the greatest in the kingdom. It is the same hand moving in the same direction. The assembly is told to walk now by the measure the Father will judge by on that day.
cards.s_text: Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this little child, the same is greatest in the kingdom of heaven.
cards.t_text: Yahuah (God) has cast down the thrones of proud princes, and set up the meek in their stead.

cards.note: *Pride is hateful before Yahuah (God) and man: and by both does one commit iniquity.* (Ecclesiasticus 10:7). *At the same time came the disciples unto Yahusha (Jesus), saying, Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?* (Matthew 18:1). Sirach names pride as hateful before Yahuah (God) and man both, the root from which iniquity grows on either side. The disciples came to Yahusha (Jesus) asking who would be greatest in the kingdom; Mark records that they had been disputing it on the road. The question itself was the disposition Sirach warned against, and the King answered it by setting a child in their midst. The kingdom does not rank the way the kingdoms of the earth do.
cards.s_text: At the same time came the disciples unto Yahusha (Jesus), saying, Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?
cards.t_text: Pride is hateful before Yahuah (God) and man: and by both does one commit iniquity.

cards.note: *You madest Adam, and gavest him Eve his wife for an helper and stay: of them came mankind: you have said, It is not good that man should be alone; let us make to him an aid like to himself.* (Tobit 8:6). *Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore Elohim (God) hath joined together, let not man put asunder.* (Matthew 19:6). On his wedding night Tobias prays the creation back over his marriage: you made Adam and gave him Eve for a helper, and from them came mankind. When the Pharisees pressed Yahusha (Jesus) about divorce he went to the same place, to the beginning, and said that what Elohim (God) has joined no man may put asunder. The library and the gospel stand on the same ground: marriage is the Father's joining, not a human arrangement to be undone at preference. Malachi says he hates putting away (Malachi 2:16), and Tobias's prayer shows a young man who already knew it.
cards.s_text: Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore Elohim (God) has joined together, let not man put asunder.
cards.t_text: You madest Adam, and gavest him Eve his wife for an helper and stay: of them came mankind: you have said, It is not good that man should be alone; let us make to him an aid like to himself.

cards.note: *And blessed is the eunuch, which with his hands has wrought no iniquity, nor imagined wicked things against Yahuah (God): for to him shall be given the special gift of faith, and an inheritance in the temple of Yahuah (God) more acceptable to his mind.* (Wisdom of Solomon 3:14). *For there are some eunuchs, which were so born from their mother’s womb: and there are some eunuchs, which were made eunuchs of men: and there be eunuchs, which have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven’s sake. He that is able to receive it, let him receive it.* (Matthew 19:12). Wisdom blesses the eunuch who has kept his hands clean and promises him the special gift of faith and an inheritance in the house of Yahuah (God). Isaiah had said it first — *even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters* (Isaiah 56:5). Yahusha (Jesus) speaks of eunuchs who have made themselves so for the kingdom of heaven's sake, and adds: he that is able to receive it, let him receive it. All three treat it as a gift received, not a rule imposed, which is the word both the system that made celibacy a requirement for its clergy and the system that treats the unmarried as half a life managed to miss. The inheritance is for the one to whom it is given.
cards.s_text: For there are some eunuchs, which were so born from their mother’s womb: and there are some eunuchs, which were made eunuchs of men: and there be eunuchs, which have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven’s sake. He that is able to receive it, let him receive it.
cards.t_text: And blessed is the eunuch, which with his hands has wrought no iniquity, nor imagined wicked things against Yahuah (God): for to him shall be given the special gift of faith, and an inheritance in the temple of Yahuah (God) more acceptable to his mind.

cards.note: *Have you children? instruct them, and bow down their neck from their youth.* (Ecclesiasticus 7:23). *Then were there brought unto him little children, that he should put his hands on them, and pray: and the disciples rebuked them.* (Matthew 19:13). Sirach puts children on the list of a man's responsibilities: if you have them, instruct them and bend their necks from their youth. The parents in Matthew 19:13 are doing that when they bring their little ones to Yahusha (Jesus) for his hands and his prayer; it is the Torah's own charge to teach the children carried out in the plainest way, bringing them to the one who teaches. The disciples rebuked the parents, and the Messiah rebuked the disciples, because the bringing was right. Instruction begins with whom you bring your children to.
cards.s_text: Then were there brought unto him little children, that he should put his hands on them, and pray: and the disciples rebuked them.
cards.t_text: Have you children? instruct them, and bow down their neck from their youth.

cards.note: *Hear me your father, O children, and do thereafter, that you may be safe.* (Ecclesiasticus 3:1). *But Yahusha (Jesus) said, Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven.* (Matthew 19:14). Sirach's picture of safety is children who hear their father and do what he says. Yahusha (Jesus) says the kingdom of heaven is of such, and he says it while his own disciples are forbidding the little ones to come. The kingdom belongs to children not because children are innocent but because a child hears his father's voice and comes when he is called; that is the disposition the kingdom is made of. Hearing is how the Father's children are shown to be his, and the one who hears and does thereafter is the one Sirach says will be safe.
cards.s_text: But Yahusha (Jesus) said, Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven.
cards.t_text: Hear me your father, O children, and do thereafter, that you may be safe.

cards.note: *And when he had called him, he said, My son, when I am dead, bury me; and despise not your mother, but honour her all the days of your life, and do that which shall please her, and grieve her not.* (Tobit 4:3). *And he laid his hands on them, and departed thence.* (Matthew 19:15). Tobit calls his son to him before he dies and hands him the commandments — honour your mother, bury me, walk uprightly — which is a father's blessing in the old form.
